  - Each situation has its own exit code.

- **A media stream the peers rejected became a media endpoint.**
  - [RFC 3264](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3264.html) sets a port of
    zero for three purposes:
    - To reject an offered stream.
    - To terminate an existing one.
    - To say a stream is not wanted.
  - All three mean no media will arrive there.
  - sipnab registered an endpoint for it anyway.
    - A call that declined video carried a video endpoint.
    - A re-INVITE tearing a stream down registered the teardown as a setup.
  - Two other places in the tree already read a zero port as a rejection.
    - The one function that creates endpoints did not.
  - Measured against the real corpus:
    - 3,233 media descriptions across four captures.
    - 7 of them rejected.
  - sipnab still parses the rejected description.
    - It is the evidence that a rejection happened.
    - Only the stream link is refused.

## [0.5.166] - 2026-09-11

### Added

- **`--seccomp enforce` refuses every system call outside a derived allowlist,
  which finishes the syscall sandbox.**
  - All four steps of its design now ship.
  - A call the list does not carry ends the process.
    - The kernel log records the number.
    - It ends the process because an `EPERM` from the output path would
      produce a run that captures happily and writes nothing.
  - **It reads its allowlist from `SIPNAB_SECCOMP_ALLOWLIST` and refuses without
    one.**
    - No list ships in the binary for it to fall back on.
    - That is a measurement, not caution.
    - The reference list settled across 16 run shapes and 29,048 records on one
      machine.
    - It killed the process on the first run on another machine of the same
      architecture.
    - An allowlist is per-host.
  - Produce yours with `scripts/derive-seccomp-allowlist.sh`, on the host that
    runs the capture.
  - Default off, as every mode here is.

- **`scripts/derive-seccomp-allowlist.sh` turns the syscall derivation from a
  judgement call into a measurement.**
  - The syscall sandbox's last step is an enforcing filter.
  - It has stayed last because a mis-derived allowlist kills the process on a
    capture box.
  - This script runs the shapes and streams the kernel records.
  - It returns a verdict, not a list.
  - It refuses more often than it answers. It refuses all of these:
    - A log the kernel dropped records in.
    - A log with no records at all.
    - A union still growing at the last shape.
  - Its success verdict is `SETTLED`, never `COMPLETE`.
    - Two quiet shapes mean those shapes stopped finding calls.
    - They do not mean that no shape would.
  - The first real run:
    - Six shapes.
    - 10,124 records.
    - No loss.
    - A union of 22 syscalls.
  - One live shape added six calls no offline shape made.

    - That is what an unexercised surface looks like.
    - It is why the enforcing filter is still not here.

### Fixed

- **`--seccomp log` sent operators to a log that silently drops records.**
  - On a host with no audit daemon, the records fall back to the kernel ring
    buffer.
  - That buffer is rate limited.
  - The kernel reports the loss as
    `kauditd_printk_skb: N callbacks suppressed`, and nothing else does.
  - Measured while deriving sipnab's own syscall set from a twenty-second
    capture:
    - 50 records arrived.
    - Roughly 1,700 were dropped.
  - It loses them a second way as well, and that way announces nothing.
    - The ring buffer wraps.
    - So reading the log after a run keeps only the last few hundred records.
    - After a twenty-second capture, reading the buffer returned 12 distinct
      syscalls.
    - Streaming the same shape returned 21.
  - Short is the dangerous direction.
    - The artifact being derived is an allowlist for an enforcing filter.
    - A filter missing a call ends the process making it.
    - So nine missing entries is nine ways to kill a capture.

  - The flag's help and the startup line now do four things:
    - Name both losses.
    - Say which one is silent.
    - Carry what the loss measured.
    - Say to stream the records rather than read them afterwards.

## [0.5.165] - 2026-09-11

### Added

- **`--seccomp log` records every system call this process makes, and allows
  every one.**

  - The syscall sandbox's design puts the enforcing filter last.
    - A mis-derived allowlist kills the process on a capture box.
    - It would do so during the incident the capture was started for.
  - The step before it is an instrument.
    - It is a seccomp filter whose only action is `SECCOMP_RET_LOG`.
    - So the allowlist can be derived from evidence instead of guessed.
  - It denies nothing and protects nothing.
    - The flag's help, the startup line and the status type all say so.
    - They do not let "seccomp active" imply a control.
  - Where the records land forks by host.
    - The guidance names both routes, because naming one is worse than naming
      none.
    - `auditctl -s` prints a connected audit daemon's pid.
      The records are then in `ausearch -m SECCOMP`.
    - A pid of 0 means no daemon.
      The records are then in `dmesg`.
  - Point it at a bounded offline run.
    - A live capture emits one record per received packet.
  - The filter is synchronized across every thread.
    - By default, seccomp covers the installing thread and its future
      children.
    - sipnab installs after the capture thread is spawned.
    - Without synchronization, the instrument would have recorded everything
      except the thread running libpcap.
  - Its own tests carried the hazard the feature is sequenced around.
    - Two child roles installed a denying filter.
    - They allow-listed, by hand, the syscalls the Rust runtime needed to
      report the verdict.
    - That list was derived on one architecture.
    - It was incomplete on the other, and it broke the build.
  - Neither role has an allowlist now.
    - One reports through a raw exit-group call, with nothing between it and
      the install.
    - The other asks the kernel per-thread whether a filter is in force.
      It does not try to be denied.

### Fixed

- **A unit test comparing this crate's filter instruction against the kernel's
  broke the macOS build.**
  - `libc::sock_filter` does not exist off Linux.
  - The comparison carried no target gate.
  - The local check that exists for this class could not see it.
    - It compiles the tree with the target values swapped.
    - That changes what `cfg` selects, but not which `libc` is linked.
    - So a type that is simply absent elsewhere still resolves.
  - The scanner that CAN see it now knows both classic-BPF types.
  - Un-gating the test fails it.

- **The DTLS detector spent neither length rule the RFCs give it, on a decision
  that deletes the packet.**
  - `is_dtls` checked a content type and a version and nothing else.
  - So it accepted a datagram whose first three bytes happened to read that
    way, whatever its length field claimed.
  - Both remaining rules are stated:
    - [RFC 6347](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6347.html) says each record
      must fit within a single datagram.
    - Its length field is the TLS 1.2 one.
      [RFC 5246](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5246.html) bounds it at
      2^14 + 2048.
  - The two errors here are not symmetric.
    That is the argument for tightening.
    - A wrong yes makes the pipeline consume the datagram.
      The packet leaves the analysis entirely.
    - A wrong no is inert.
      Every content type DTLS uses carries the wrong version bits for RTP.
      So a refused datagram has nowhere else to go.
  - Measured against 3,962,333 real UDP datagrams first:
    - 93 were accepted as DTLS.
    - Neither rule refuses one of them.

- **The RTCP padding rule shipped in 0.5.164 never reached the capture path,
  and its release note said otherwise.**

  - That note read: "one more bit of separation on the classifier that decides
    RTP against RTCP for every datagram on a media port".
  - The rule landed on `rtp::rtcp::looks_like_rtcp`.
    Nothing in the capture path calls it.
  - The classifier a captured datagram actually reaches kept a private copy of
    the length logic.
    - Nobody told that copy about the rule.
    - So on a muxed port, sipnab went on accepting compounds
      [RFC 3550](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3550.html) forbids.
  - The copy is gone.
  - The muxed verdict comes from the one function that holds the content rules.
  - A test fails if the two ever answer differently again.
  - Operators running 0.5.164 have the classifier described in its release
    note only from this release on.

- **The RTCP decoder now says why it does not require the sub-packet lengths to
  total the datagram.**
  - RFC 3550 Appendix A.2 recommends that check.
    sipnab does not apply it.
  - Measured against 4,904,975 real UDP datagrams:
    - Applying it would refuse 67 of the 11,696 accepted as RTCP.
    - 61 are SRTCP.
      Their cleartext header is followed by ciphertext and an authentication
      tag that cannot chain.
    - 6 leave a ragged tail of one to three bytes.
  - Nothing else is refused.
  - So the check's whole effect would be to send encrypted call control down
    the RTP path and invent a media stream from it.

- **Two release gates disagreed about which files phase two of a release
  touches.**
  - The eBPF load record became a required part of phase two when LIVE3 landed.
    - `published_version` cannot name a release with no recorded verification.
  - Nobody told the classifier that recognizes a phase-two commit.
    - It read the record as ordinary work.
    - The delivery gates refused the one commit the flow is supposed to
      produce.
    - That left a bypass as the only route.
  - Both now read one constant.
  - The tests drive the states this checkout cannot reach.

## [0.5.164] - 2026-09-10

### Added

- **`--sandbox` bounds which files a capture can reach, using Landlock.**
  - sipnab's parsers are safe Rust.
  - libpcap is C.
    - It touches every untrusted byte first.
    - It runs in the address space holding TLS key material and bearer tokens.
  - The privilege drop stops that address space reaching other users' files.
    - It does nothing about the files this user can already read.
  - With `--sandbox best-effort`, a read or write comes back `EACCES` when it is
    outside all of these:
    - The input set.
    - The output directory.
    - The keylog.
    - The crash directory.
  - `--sandbox required` refuses to capture when no sandbox is in force.
  - Default off, so no existing run changes.
  - **Sockets are not bounded.**
    - The startup line says so, rather than letting "sandboxed" imply it.
    - Landlock's network rules reach TCP bind and connect only.
    - They would miss the HEP UDP listener and the pre-drop raw socket
      entirely.
  - **Nothing here can end a run.**
    - Landlock denies an open. It does not signal.
    - A kernel without Landlock degrades to a warning, never a refusal, unless
      `required` says otherwise.

### Fixed

- **A HEP datagram with an impossible length was refused for the wrong reason.**
  - The total-length field counts the header it sits in.
    - So a value below six cannot be true.

  - Such packets were already refused.
  - The message said they lacked a source address.
    - That sent an operator to the sender's addressing, not to its length
      field.
  - The refusal now names the length.
  - A packet carrying no chunks at all is refused the same way.

- **The TLS record walk accepted zero-length fragments both RFCs forbid.**
  - No conformant peer emits a zero-length Handshake, Alert or
    ChangeCipherSpec fragment.
  - The walk took the declared zero at face value.
  - Application Data is deliberately exempt.
    - Both RFCs permit a zero-length fragment there as a traffic-analysis
      countermeasure.

  - The walk stops at a forbidden record rather than skipping it.
    - A record layer that resynchronizes on untrusted bytes walks off into a
      payload.

- **The WebSocket detector accepted a length encoding
  [RFC 6455](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455.html) forbids.**
  - The RFC requires the shortest length form that can carry a payload.
  - The detector took the extended forms at face value:
    - A two-byte length declaring fewer than 126 bytes read as a frame.
    - So did an eight-byte length declaring anything two bytes could hold.
  - That is 126 values of the 16-bit space spent.
    - The detector's job is telling a frame from any other TCP payload that
      starts with two plausible bytes.
  - The detector and the unwrapper now read one rule.

    - So neither can accept what the other refuses.

- **A test asserting an exact count of dropped oversize headers could read
  another test's work.**
  - The counter is a process statistic.
    - That is right for the product.
    - It is hostile to a test that resets it and then reads it.
  - Any test parsing an over-cap header in parallel lands between the two
    operations.
  - One did, and the test read 45 where it had just reset to zero.
  - Every test that can move that counter is now serialized on one key.
  - A gate derives the list from the source.
    It does not trust anyone to remember it.

- **The RTCP classifier ignored the padding rule RFC 3550 states as a MUST.**
  - Padding may only appear on the last packet of a compound.
  - So a first sub-packet that does not fill the datagram cannot carry the
    padding bit.
  - That is one more bit of separation on the classifier that decides RTP
    against RTCP for every datagram on a media port.
  - A lone packet that fills the datagram is the last one, and may still pad.

- **The LLMNR detector left five RFC-mandated zero bits unspent.**
  - LLMNR is bare DNS with no magic cookie.
  - So a port number is the only strong evidence that a datagram is a name
    lookup.
    - Otherwise it may be something that landed on 5355 by accident.
  - [RFC 4795](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4795.html) has two rules for a
    query:
    - It requires RCODE zero.
    - It forbids the truncation bit.
  - Neither was checked.
  - Both checks are query-only.
    - A responder sets RCODE.
    - The RFC forbids truncation only on queries.

- **The STUN decoder accepted a message length
  [RFC 8489](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8489.html) says never occurs.**
  - Every attribute is padded to a multiple of four.
  - So the length field's last two bits are always zero.
  - The RFC names that as a way to tell STUN from other protocols.
  - The decoder did not check it.
    - The decoder shares ports with RTP.
    - It has already claimed a GTPv2-C datagram as an RTP stream once.

  - This adds two more bits of collision resistance.

    - They come from the specification, not invented.

- **A new format gate reported "unformatted" when rustfmt was simply absent.**
  - CI's feature-matrix jobs install the toolchain without the rustfmt
    component.
  - So `cargo fmt --check` exited non-zero with an empty diff.
  - The gate read that exit status as a finding about the code.
    - It reported both excluded packages as unformatted, with nothing
      underneath.
    - main went red over code that was correctly formatted.
  - The verdict is now a three-way decision:
    - A diff is unformatted.
    - An empty diff with a non-zero exit is a checker that could not run.
  - In the second case, the gate says so and declines to judge.

- **The tag prompt did not name the two obligations that only exist after
  publishing.**
  - Both the binary-ceiling record and the eBPF load record key on
    `published_version`.
    - So neither can pass before the artifacts exist.
  - The only thing that tells a maintainer about them is the prompt `pre-push`
    prints when a tag goes up.
  - That prompt named two of the four steps.
  - A test now holds the prompt to the gates.

### Added

- **The install page says which capture backends each artifact can reach.**
  - libpcap picks a backend from the device name.
  - sipnab passes the name through.
  - So whether `--device netmap:eth0` works depends on the libpcap behind the
    binary.
  - The two artifact families differ:
    - The static musl tarballs embed libpcap 1.10.6 with the netmap module.
    - The gnu tarballs, the packages and the Docker image link the host's
      libpcap.
    - Debian builds that libpcap without the module.

  - Two operators running the same command on the same release got different
    answers.
    Nothing said why.
  - The release now refuses to publish a musl artifact whose embedded libpcap
    lost the module.

### Fixed

- **A metrics test could only report a port number when it failed.**
  - Its probe gave up after six seconds.
  - It asserted "nothing answered on `<addr>`".
  - That reads the same in three cases:
    - sipnab was slow to bind.
    - sipnab exited at startup.
    - sipnab lost the ephemeral port to another process.
  - The test now keeps the child's stderr.
  - It stops the moment the process exits, rather than burning the rest of the
    budget.
  - It waits thirty seconds instead of six.
    - A cold runner spawning a freshly linked binary is slower than the old
      ceiling allowed.
  - It failed exactly that way on a macOS runner.
    The log said nothing more than the port.

- **The eBPF kernel source was never formatted, and five gates said it was.**
  - `cargo fmt --all` reaches workspace members.
  - `fuzz/` and `bpf/` are excluded from the workspace on purpose.
  - So five gates reported clean formatting for a package none of them had
    looked at:
    - Both hooks.
    - CI.
    - The preflight script.
    - The prepare-commit fixer.
  - `bpf/src/main.rs` had an unformatted array the whole time.
  - Every gate now names the excluded packages.
  - A test derives that list from the manifests.
    It does not trust the gates to remember it.

## [0.5.163] - 2026-09-10

### Added

- **The TUI shows the wideband MOS for AMR-WB streams.**
  - An AMR-WB call had two numbers, depending on which surface you read:
    - REST and MCP carried `MOS_CQEW` on the ITU-T G.107.1 scale.
    - The stream-detail pane showed the narrowband `MOS_CQE`.
      - That score anchors 35.8 R-points away.
      - It cannot score a wideband codec at all.
  - The pane now carries a `MOS_CQEW` row.
    - The row names the scale, the mode and the listening context.
  - It has no quality band and no color on purpose.

    - The bands calibrate against the narrowband scale.
  - A stream nobody attempted to score gets no row.
  - A stream sipnab cannot score says why in words.

- **`scripts/verify-bpf-load.sh`**
  - It verifies that a published artifact's eBPF program loads and attaches.
  - It runs on a host with root and kernel BTF.
  - It downloads the release tarball.
  - It checks the tarball against the checksum published beside it.
  - It judges the run.
  - The suite cannot cover loading.
    - Loading needs privileges a test process must never acquire.
    - Building was never the half that broke.

- **Continuous fuzzing with a corpus that survives between runs.**
  - ClusterFuzzLite builds the eighteen fuzz targets in the OSS-Fuzz Rust
    builder image.
  - It runs them on a schedule:
    - Batch fuzzing daily.
    - Corpus pruning daily.
    - A coverage report weekly.
  - The existing weekly `cargo-fuzz` run starts from the tracked seeds every
    time.

    - So everything libFuzzer learns is discarded.
    - This keeps it.
  - Pull-request fuzzing and continuous builds are deliberately absent.
    - Without continuous builds, pull-request fuzzing reports pre-existing
      crashes as though the change introduced them.
  - The build was proven in the real image before being trusted.
  - Five defects surfaced only there:
    - A builder image whose Rust is a year older than this crate's
      `rust-version`.
    - A `rustup default` silently overridden by the image's own
      `RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN`.
    - A toolchain profile missing the standard library source OSS-Fuzz copies
      out of it.
    - A `.dockerignore` that excluded the seed corpora.
    - A runner image without libpcap.
      It rejected all eighteen targets from a build which had exited zero.
  - Each is now a gate.

## [0.5.162] - 2026-09-10

### Fixed

- **The eBPF uprobe backend did not load on a current kernel, on every release
  artifact that ships it.**
  - `--uprobe-backend bpf` failed with `verifier
  rejected the uprobe: BPF_PROG_LOAD returned Permission denied`.
  - The verifier's own line was `R2 unbounded memory access`.
  - It failed loudly.
    - An operator got a refusal naming both libraries and the symbol.
    - It was not a capture that silently held nothing.
    - But the capability was absent.
  - **The cause was the nightly compiler, not the code.**

    - The read length was already clamped.
    - A newer nightly spills the clamped value to the stack.
    - It then reloads it into the argument register.
    - The verifier does not keep the range across that round trip.
    - It sees `0..=0x7fffffff` and refuses.
    - An older nightly kept the value in a register and loaded fine.
      So nothing noticed.
  - This was established by elimination on one host and one kernel.
    - The linker version changes the object, not the outcome.
    - The feature set produces a byte-identical object, because the kernel
      crate is separate.

  - The fix puts the bound **at the instruction the verifier checks**.
    - It is a mask against a constant, immediately before the read.
    - No register allocator can hoist it away from the call it guards.
  - The clamp target moves to `MAX_PAYLOAD - 1`, so the mask is exact.
    - Masking a value that can equal the buffer size would read nothing on
      precisely the largest write.
  - A write of exactly `MAX_PAYLOAD` is now truncated by one byte and flagged
    as such.
    - Before, it was copied whole and unflagged.
  - Verified in both directions on the two compilers reachable here:
    - On the one that failed, the object goes from rejected to attached.
    - On the one that worked, it stays attached.
  - Either result alone would not separate a fix from a coincidence.

### Removed

- **The `rust-clippy` analysis workflow.**
  - CI already runs clippy at a stricter scope:
    `--workspace --all-features --all-targets` with `-D warnings`.
  - CI fails on any warning.
  - So the existing gate has already refused every finding that workflow could
    report.
  - Its output went to code scanning.
    - This project fails CI on any open alert.
    - So a finding would have left the clippy job green.
    - It would have failed CI in a different job, over an alert in a different
      tab.

### Changed

- **The toolchain moves to Rust 1.98.1, and three hand-rolled routines become
  standard-library calls.**
  - `[T]::subslice_range` is now the whole body of the mapped reader's
    `offset_within_mapping`.
    - The old code cast two pointers to `usize` and compared the integers.
    - That was correct in practice.
    - To be correct, it threw the pointers' provenance away.
  - `str::substr_range` replaced pointer arithmetic in the filter parser.
    - That parser's own comment records the bug the arithmetic caused on
      multibyte input.
    - It refuses a string that is not part of this one.
    - In that case, the arithmetic produced a plausible index.
  - `str::strip_circumfix` replaced a prefix strip fed into a suffix strip in
    the termination parser.
  - The bump is not a drop-in.
    - Clippy gained `chunks_exact_to_as_chunks` in 1.98.
    - That lint is fatal under this project's warnings-as-errors.
    - Three call sites moved to `as_chunks::<2>()`.
    - The internet checksum reads its word as `from_be_bytes(*pair)`, not as
      two indexed loads.
  - Behavior is unchanged in every case.
    - Both forms drop a trailing odd byte.

### Added

- **`scripts/check-file.sh` runs the per-file gates in about a second**
  - It runs on the files you just wrote.
  - It runs these gates:
    - vale.
    - codespell.
    - The British-spelling sweep.
    - rustfmt.
    - A parse for shell and Python.
  - The commit hook is the entry check on a commit.
    - It is not the mechanism for discovering a misspelling.
    - In one session, eight round trips through it went to defects of that
      class.
  - Every decision in it is borrowed, not restated.
    - vale and codespell come from `scripts/prose-gates.sh`.
      - These are the same runners the hooks call.
      - They include the version pin that decides whether a vale run is
        evidence about CI at all.
      - Those runners gained an optional path argument for it.
    - The forbidden-word list and its exemptions are parsed out of the gate
      that owns them.
      - So the script catches a word added there without a second edit.

## [0.5.161] - 2026-09-09

### Added

- **The harness stops throwing its captures away.**
  - Every run produced traffic no test would ever see again.
    - `harness/captures/*.pcap` is ignored.
    - Only `.gitkeep` is tracked.
  - A capture with no recorded provenance cannot be safely promoted
    afterwards.
    - Nobody can later establish which scenario produced it.
    - Nobody can establish which media anchor was in force.
    - That is what stopped captures being kept.
  - `harness/scripts/capture.sh` records that provenance at the time of
    capture.
  - It **refuses to run without `--pins`**.
    - Deciding what a capture is for is cheap while the stack is up.
    - It is impossible a fortnight later.
  - It reads the anchor off the running container, not from `.env`.
    - Those drift the moment anyone runs `make up ANCHOR=x`.
  - It captures with `tcpdump`, not `sipnab -O`.
    - A fixture written by the program under test cannot contradict it.
  - `harness/scripts/promote.sh` does three things:
    - It moves a capture into `tests/pcap-samples/`.
    - It writes the capture's entry in `PROVENANCE.md`.
    - It re-checks the bytes against the sha256 the record names.
  - The first fixture is `opensips-direct-media-proxy-view.pcap`.
    - It is a real OpenSIPS 3.6.7 call with no media anchor, captured at the
      proxy.
    - It has a complete dialog and **zero RTP streams**.
    - The media went endpoint to endpoint.
  - The zero is the assertion, not an absence of one.

    - The SDP offers PCMA.
    - A reconstruction that trusts the offer rather than the wire would report
      a stream.
    - That stream would have a codec, a direction and a MOS that nothing
      measured.
  - Two gates hold it up:
    - One requires every committed fixture to carry a manifest entry, or to
      sit on the enumerated list of the 36 that predate the rule.
    - One asserts what the entry claims.

- **sipnab reads which AMR mode a sender actually used, off the RTP payload
  header.**
  - `crate::rtp::emodel_wb` has been able to score AMR-WB on the wideband
    E-model since it was written. It has:
    - The G.113 tables for all nine modes.
    - The G.107.1 equations.
    - An SDP `mode-set` reader.
  - Nothing in the source had ever called any of it.
    - It needs an input the codec name does not carry.
  - The nine modes span `Ie,WB` 1 to 41.
    - That is about 4.49 down to 3.51 MOS.
    - So "AMR-WB" alone leaves a full MOS point of ambiguity.
  - A `mode-set` pins nothing unless it names exactly one mode.

    - Real VoLTE signaling rarely does that.
  - The new `crate::rtp::amr` reads
    [RFC 4867](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4867.html)'s payload header in
    both packings.
    - In the bandwidth-efficient packing, the frame type straddles an octet
      boundary.
    - In the octet-aligned packing, it sits in a table-of-contents octet.
  - So the packing is an explicit argument with **no default**.
    - Reading one as the other returns a plausible mode, not an error.
  - Interleaving is refused outright.
    - Its `ILL`/`ILP` field moves every offset.
  - Comfort noise carries no mode, and sipnab never records it as one.
    - AMR-WB frame type 9 is a silence descriptor.
    - Narrowband frame type 8 is one too.
    - That is at the index that means 23.85 kbit/s on the wideband table.
  - `GET /v1/streams` and the MCP stream surfaces carry two new keys:
    - `amr_mode_kbps` exists only when every readable frame used the same mode.
    - `amr_modes_observed` says how many distinct modes the payloads carried.
      It is absent, not zero, when nothing was read.
  - Both absent means sipnab could not read the payloads.
  - A count above one with no mode means sipnab read them and the sender
    moved.
  - An endpoint learned with no media description pins no packing at all.
    - RFC 4867 settles what an SDP that stayed *silent* means.
    - It says nothing about an SDP nobody saw.

- **A recipe for reading a capture eCapture wrote, with no sipnab
  configuration at all**
  - It is cookbook 7i.
  - `ecapture tls -m pcap` writes the real encrypted frames.
  - It embeds the master secrets as a pcapng Decryption Secrets Block.
  - So `sipnab -I file.pcapng` decrypts it with no `--keylog` and no flags.
  - Measured end to end against a complete TLS 1.3 dialog.
    - That dialog's process set no keylog of its own.

- **A troubleshooting section for encrypted SIP that does not decrypt**
  - The page had none before.
  - It is built around the one line that separates the cases:
    `TLS decryption active:`.
  - It covers the two silent keylog-pipe failures by symptom, not by version.
    - A build that predates their fix reports nothing at all.

- **The IPC wire D16 specified**, and the reason the fork stops there.

  - The wire is four bytes of big-endian length, then that many bytes of JSON.
  - The length is checked before anything is allocated.
  - A clean end of stream is told apart from a truncated frame.
  - Nothing speaks it yet.
    Both the code and the backlog say so.
  - `TransmitPermit` is a zero-sized proof token that cannot cross a pipe.

    - So a forked scanner-kill child takes its capability from the inherited
      raw socket instead.
    - That is a different design from the one `PI2` described.

### Changed

- **The benchmarks page and the throughput gate now measure one binary, and a
  test says so.**
  - `bench/baseline.json` recorded 0.5.122 at 3.25M packets per second on four
    cores.
  - The page published 3.23M for the same release.
  - Neither was a transcription slip.
    - One gate required the page to name a *released artifact*.
    - The baseline file required *a local release build of the recorded
      commit*.
      The nightly gate has to catch a regression the day it lands.
  - These were two honest measurements of two different programs.
    - They were 0.6% apart, inside the page's own noise floor.
  - Re-measured on 0.5.160 on the documented host:
    - 1.05M at one core.
    - 2.63M at two cores.
    - **3.56M** at four cores.
    - 3.13M at eight cores.
  - These are published as the lowest of three replicates, not the median.
    - So a reader who re-runs the harness meets or beats the figure.

  - Four cores is the peak, and **eight is slower**, in every replicate.

    - The page previously said the opposite.
    - That came from a session whose table it never published.
  - The four-core figure reproduces the backlog's own independently recorded
    3.56M to the digit.
  - `bench/baseline.json` holds all of these:
    - Every replicate.
    - Every peak resident set.
    - The whole carrier-scale sweep.
  - Figures that resolved to no record were deleted, not carried forward.
  - A single test binds the committed figure to three places:
    - The published cell of both hand-maintained copies of the page.
    - The homepage tile.
      It now derives its expected value instead of restating it.

- **`ecapture tls -m pcap` no longer described as emitting plaintext.**
  - Cookbook 7e declined it.
    - It said it would write "capture files whose packets never existed on the
      wire".
  - The backlog said it "writes decrypted traffic as pcapng".
  - Running it settled both.
    - It writes the real encrypted frames with the secrets embedded.
    - That is the artifact 7e argues for.

- **Advertised tool schemas use a spelling every MCP client can read.**
  - The Inspector's `--strict` lint reported 172 findings across 47 tools, in
    two classes.
  - Three were `serde_json::Value` fields described as nothing at all:
    - A vCon container, twice.
    - The capture caveats.
  - Those now say `type:
  object`, the one thing always true of them.
  - The other 169 were `type` as an array.
    - That is what `schemars` writes for an optional field.
    - It is legal JSON Schema.
    - Several clients cannot read that spelling.
      - They take `type` as a single string.
      - They either drop the constraint or refuse the whole tool.
      - A refused tool is one the agent simply does not have.

  - Those unions are collapsed on **input** schemas, once, where the router is
    assembled.
  - They are not collapsed on output schemas.
    - sipnab writes an explicit `null` for an absent optional field.
    - Collapsing there would advertise a schema its own responses violate.
    - The existing payload-versus-schema test caught that within a minute of
      the first draft.
  - The input side is also where the cost falls.
    - A client validates arguments before calling.
  - 172 findings become 83.
    - Every one that remains is that single waived class.
    - Nothing is on an input schema.
    - Nothing is described as anything at all.
  - No continuous-integration job runs the Inspector.
    - A test asserts the property it checks offline, against the live wire.
    - The walk is driven on a planted fixture, so it cannot pass by matching
      nothing.
    - An unpinned package fetched on every push would re-derive in minutes
      what a test settles in seconds.
    - Adding one is the opposite of how this project treats its tools.

### Fixed

- **The OpenAPI document described a stream field the response had been
  carrying.**
  - `dialog_assertion` was missing from the schema mirror in
    `src/output/api.rs`.
  - `GET /v1/streams` served it.
  - Nothing compares that struct against the model it describes.

## [0.5.160] - 2026-09-09

### Changed

- **The published binary-size ceiling moves from 15 MB to 16 MB, and the
  mitigation that was supposed to warn about it did not.**
  - The release build refused this version's x86_64-musl binary at 15,747,848 bytes.
  - That is 19,208 over the 15 MB the homepage advertises.
  - Measured from the shipped stripped binaries:
    - 15,612,680 at 0.5.157.
    - 15,608,584 at 0.5.158.
    - 15,629,064 at 0.5.159.
    - 15,747,848 here.

  - So 0.5.159 shipped with 99,576 bytes of headroom.
  - It was one ordinary release from tipping, and nothing said so.
  - The same gate failed a release at 0.5.139.
    - The mitigation chosen then was the ceiling's own comment.
    - The comment records the measurement behind every ceiling MOVE.
    - The goal was that "the remaining headroom is readable without building anything".
    - It was not readable.
    - Nothing required a refresh of the record between moves.
    - So it still described 0.5.138 while three releases went past.
  - Two tests replace that.
    - One demands a measurement line for the release currently published.
      - So nobody can cut a release without re-measuring.
    - One fails while the margin is thin.
      - So the ceiling rises at the release that gets close.
      - It does not rise at the tag that publishes nothing.
    - Both read measurement LINES rather than grepping the block.
      - The first draft did grep it.
      - It passed against a record with every measurement deleted.
      - The version was named in a sentence and the byte counts were in the prose.

  - Shrinking was considered and rejected, for the reason it was rejected at 0.5.139.
    - The release profile already runs link-time optimization.
    - It also runs a single codegen unit, symbol stripping and abort-on-panic.
    - The only lever left trades the throughput the benchmarks page publishes.

- **A decision that captures must never be committed is now a gate, not a
  note.**

  - Five LTE captures entered the private corpus.
  - They are the reason anyone found a GTPv2-C control message reported as an
    RTP stream with a confident `mos: 1.0`.
  - They stay private for two independent reasons:
    - The source page states no license at all.
      - Absence of terms is "all rights reserved" rather than permission.
    - They carry a real IMEI in a `+sip.instance` URN.
      - They also carry an IMSI-derived subscriber identity.
  - That decision was written down and enforced by nothing.
    - A backlog entry does not survive a `git add`.
    - The risk is a capture landing in a fixtures directory because somebody was moving fast.
    - At that point it is in a public repository's history permanently.
  - The gate is keyed on what a file CONTAINS, never on the five names.
    - A denylist of names passes the sixth capture.
    - The sixth is the one nobody thought about.
  - It walks the whole repository rather than the test tree.

    - Four captures ship from outside the test tree.
    - The sample the browser analyzer loads reaches more people than any fixture.
  - It also says what it does not cover.
    - Two of those five hold roughly 19 MB of one person's DNS queries and TLS SNI.
    - That is as disqualifying as the IMEI.
    - It has no crisp byte pattern, because a fixture may legitimately carry DNS.
    - That half stays a human decision, and the gate does not pretend otherwise.

- **`--retain-audio` no longer requires `--mcp`.**
  - The constraint was right when it was written.
    - The MCP `export_audio` tool was the only thing that could read the
      retained buffers back.
    - Retaining without it would have spent the memory on audio nothing in the run could reach.
    - That would be a flag that parses and does nothing.
  - The amplitude measurement above reads the same buffers on `--call-report`
    and `--json-dialogs`.
    - So the constraint would have kept the one finding that needs samples behind a server.
    - Nobody analyzing a pcap wants to start that server.
  - The objection it answered now has a different answer: the test asserts the EFFECT.
    - A plain batch run with the flag must produce the measurement.
    - It must not merely accept the argument.
  - Retention is still opt-in.
  - `--mcp` alone still never arms it.
    - Enabling a server is not consent to hold call audio.

### Fixed

- **A vulnerability that was accepted in writing came back wearing a different
  number, and turned main red.**
  - `extract-zip` reached the Lighthouse tooling four levels down:
    - `@lhci/cli` to `lighthouse` to `puppeteer-core` to `@puppeteer/browsers`.
  - Its newest published release IS the vulnerable one.

    - So there was no upgrade to take.

  - The first advisory was accepted deliberately.
    - The reasoning and an expiry condition were written down.
  - Then a second symlink advisory landed on that same version.
    - Code scanning opened an alert.
    - The CI gate that refuses open alerts failed on main.
  - That is what an acceptance cannot cover.
    - It is written against the problem known on the day.
    - The next one arrives without asking.
  - The package is gone instead of accepted again.
    - `@puppeteer/browsers` 3.0.2 replaced `extract-zip` with `tar-fs`.
    - So an npm `override` to that major removes it from the lockfile entirely.
  - Lighthouse still collects.
    - Every symbol `puppeteer-core` imports from that package exists in 3.x.
    - A real collection run was made against the override before it was committed.
  - The acceptance MECHANISM went with it, on the instruction its own test carried.
    - An acceptance table with nothing in it is an untested mechanism.
  - Two tests replace it, and they state the property rather than the pin:
    - One fails if `extract-zip` is installed.
    - One fails if any package still merely NAMES it.
      - A declared-but-unresolved dependency is one `npm install` away from
        being an installed one.

- **Two more doc blocks had been cut in half, in a tree no gate read.**
  - The doc-split rules ran over `src/` and nothing else.
  - `tests/` holds 5,014 doc blocks.
    - The reasoning for every gate is written down there.
    - So a split there destroys exactly the explanation somebody needs when that gate fails.
  - Two were sitting in it:
    - `tool_descriptions_do_not_instruct_the_model_to_trust_content` was
      documented, in full, as `/// what it gets back.`.
    - `every_flag_has_at_least_two_examples` had lost its first line the same way.
  - There are now five instances of one defect, across two trees.
  - The scan was always the cheap part.
  - Not pointing it at everything was the whole gap.

- **Six items shipped in 0.5.159 with their backlog checkboxes never flipped.**
  - So the backlog reported released work as open for a release.
  - Verified against the tree rather than against the release notes.

### Added

- **A gateway sending full-rate frames of digital silence passed every check
  sipnab had.**
  - The packets arrive, in sequence, in both directions, at the right rate.
  - Loss is zero and jitter is zero.
  - The MOS is 4.36 and grounded.
  - Nothing in the report says the call was silent.
  - Counting comfort-noise frames does not find it either.
    - Those frames say "I am sending silence".
    - This gateway is not saying anything.
  - Everything sipnab looked at was the envelope.
  - `--retain-audio` already decoded the payload to PCM for WAV export.
    - So the samples were in hand, and nothing looked at them.
  - Now `diagnosis.amplitude` reports two measurements on those samples.
    - It does so on every surface a media diagnosis reaches.
    - Dead-air spans below a -60 dBFS floor.
      - Measured over 100 ms windows.
      - Reported at a second or longer.
    - Hard-clip runs of three or more consecutive samples at 99% of the codec's full scale.

  - **Every threshold is a field, not a sentence in the source.**
    - Nobody can argue with a finding whose threshold lives only in the code.
    - So these values all travel in the payload beside the numbers they produced:
      - The floor.
      - The window.
      - The minimum span.
      - The clip threshold.
      - The minimum run.
  - **These are amplitude measurements and neither is a quality score.**

    - They say what the samples did.
    - A perceptual score would need a subjectively-labeled corpus.
    - That corpus does not exist here.
    - A reader could not reproduce it from the pcap to check.
  - **The clip threshold is the codec's ceiling, not the container's.**
    - G.711 decodes into a 16-bit word it never fills.
      - mu-law tops out at 32,124.
      - A-law tops out at 32,256.
    - So a test written against 32,767 never fires on the two codecs most telephony runs on.
    - sipnab reads the ceiling off the decode tables.
  - **Absent means not measured.**
    - `diagnosis.amplitude` is one optional object rather than two booleans, deliberately.
    - `dead_air: false` on a call nobody decoded reads as "checked, and fine".
    - That is the same shape of wrong answer as a MOS on a codec with no
      published impairment value.

- **The quality trend recorded how a call was going and never how good it
  was.**
  - `QualityInterval` carried a timestamp, jitter, loss and a packet count.
  - It carried no score and no verdict.
  - So the one view built to show a call changing over time was the one view
    with no judgment in it.
  - The reader had to score six minutes of five-second rows by eye.
  - Each interval now carries `mos`, `r_factor`, `verdict` and `mos_grounded`.
    - The score uses the interval's own jitter and loss.
    - It also uses the stream's resolved path delay.
  - That last part keeps a trend and the headline above it comparable.

    - They rest on one basis, resolved once.

  - Two surfaces had been computing their own:
    - The browser analyzer called the E-model directly.
    - The terminal's stream-detail pane called the E-model directly.
    - Both now go through the one scorer.
  - **`not_scorable` is a verdict, not a missing one.**

    - There are three states:
      - R at or above 70 is `acceptable`.
        - This is ITU-T G.107's boundary between "some users dissatisfied" and "many".
      - Below it is `degraded`.
      - A codec with no published or declared impairment value is `not_scorable`.
        - It gets no color at either end.
    - The boundary is a published figure rather than a tunable.

      - The operator's own bands decide what gets a COLOR on their network.
      - An exported verdict that means something different per deployment is
        worth less than no verdict.
  - **What the work found.**
    - The stream-detail pane already muted an ungrounded headline MOS.
      - It said in as many words that a band color on a placeholder is the lie
        in its most convincing form.
    - Then, three lines lower, it banded every interval of that same stream on
      the good/poor scale.
    - It also printed a confident average underneath.
    - One pane gave two answers about one number.
  - **Five seconds was also the wrong resolution.**
    - It averages away any burst shorter than itself.
    - That is the shape of the dead-air complaint an operator escalates.
    - One 90 % loss figure this project had to explain turned out to be three
      bursts of half a second.
    - `--quality-interval` and `[limits] quality_interval_secs` take 1 to 300 seconds.
  - The retention moves with it.
    - It used to be a count: 720 entries.
    - That meant an hour only while nobody moved the period.
    - At one second, those 720 entries would have been twelve minutes.
    - The operator who shortened the interval to see a half-second burst would
      have lost the other forty-eight minutes of call to find it in.
    - The hour is the setting now, and the count is derived.
    - So a finer interval costs memory and never history.

- **"Which of these 40 files holds Call-ID X" can be asked now.**
  - It could not be asked at all before.
    - `list_captures` narrows by time, which is a filter and not an answer.
    - The only way inside another file was `open_capture`.
      - It is documented **Destructive**.
      - It replaces every dialog and stream.
      - It mints a new `capture_identity` that voids every cursor the caller holds.
  - `find_in_captures` sweeps instead:
    - A scratch store per file.
    - The filter applied.
    - The loaded capture untouched.
  - **Read `complete` before believing an empty result.**
    - A sweep runs under bounds.
    - One reporting no matches has not shown the call is absent.
      - It shows only that the sweep did not find it in what it managed to read.
    - `complete` is true in exactly one case: every candidate examined and every one readable.
    - A file the sweep could not open is named in `unreadable` with its reason.
      - It is never skipped silently.
      - The file nobody could look in is exactly the one that might hold the call.
    - A match does not excuse a truncation either.
      - On a rotated spool, a call that spans a rotation is in two files.
  - There are two bounds, because they fail differently.
    - `max_files` makes the cost predictable.
    - `deadline_ms` is the one that matters.
      - A file's cost is its size, and the caller cannot see it.
    - The sweep tests the deadline before each file.

      - Tested after, the last file overruns it by its whole read.
    - There is no cancel.
      - A tool call has no channel to interrupt it.
      - So the sweep bounds itself and always returns with an account of what it covered.

- **A manager password in the clear, on a port sipnab read and never
  parsed.**
  - Asterisk's Manager Interface speaks a line protocol on TCP/5038.
  - A login is four lines of plain text: `Action: login`, `Username:`, `Secret:`.
  - sipnab already ships `--digest-leak` for a SIP digest weak enough to grind offline.
  - A manager password on the wire is the same finding class with strictly worse consequences.
    - AMI can originate calls, read configuration and run shell commands.
  - `capture_status` reported `unanalysed_sip_messages: 0` on a capture full of it.
    - That zero was honest.
    - AMI is not SIP, so there was no unparsed SIP message to count.
    - Every detector sipnab had ran on parsed SIP messages.
    - This traffic never became one.
  - `capture_status` now reports the finding, which is where the misleading zero was.
  - **It never records the secret.**
    - The `Secret:` line becomes a boolean.
    - A finding is written to logs, exported in containers and read into an agent's context.
    - The username is echoed, bounded.
      - Someone can act on a finding naming the exposed account.
      - Nobody can act on one saying "an account".
  - **It costs effectively nothing.**
    - Two byte-level prefix tests run before anything allocates.
    - The first version decoded every payload first.
      - This runs on every non-SIP TCP payload.
      - A corpus full of HTTP is exactly that.
      - The corpus gate's own wedge detector killed it twice before the fix.
    - Measured after: 106.73s against a 105.89s baseline with the hook removed.
    - That is under 1%.
  - It is not a decoder.
    - It matches a banner and a login line and records where they were.

  - The port is an observation rather than a filter.

    - So an interface moved off 5038 is still reported.
  - Sightings aggregate per address pair.
    - The account is deliberately outside the key.
    - This path runs before authentication, so the attacker chooses the field.

- **A private `Contact` nobody rewrote is now a finding, and one that WAS
  rewritten is not.**
  - A phone behind NAT registers its own private address.
  - The registrar must notice the packet came from a public address the header does not name.
  - It must then route later requests there instead.
  - When it does not, every inbound call goes to an unroutable host.
    - The phone never rings.
  - `diagnose_registration` reports the observation.
  - `describe_endpoint` reports the corroborated finding:
    - `observation`, `verdict`, `requests_to_contact`, `requests_to_source` and `is_finding`.
  - **The observation cannot be the finding.**
    - Measured against the private corpus: 1,660 of 2,226 REGISTER contacts
      carry a private host, which is 74.6%.
    - That estate works.
    - Firing on the shape alone would report three quarters of a healthy fleet.
    - Any request to the private host is a finding, not a majority of them.
      - 99 deliverable requests do not make the hundredth deliverable.

    - Silence is `no-later-requests`, never `rewritten`.
      - So a capture that ended before the first inbound call is not a clean bill of health.
  - **The tie is the registered AoR, not the address.**
    - A request the registrar sent to the private `Contact` carries no address
      belonging to the endpoint.
    - That is exactly what going to the wrong host means.
    - The first implementation matched on the endpoint's own address.
    - So it found nothing on the very case it exists for.
  - One private-address rule now serves all three callers.
    - `rtp::diagnosis` and `security::recommend` had their own copies.
    - The copies differed only on loopback.
    - Both delegate to `crate::net::is_private_address`.
    - Neither answer changed.

- **`describe_endpoint` reports which signaling stack built an endpoint's
  requests.**
  - A `User-Agent` banner names a product.
  - One product ships more than one stack.
    - `top_talkers by=ua` reports `Asterisk PBX 20.15.2` as a single row at
      100% share across 507 dialogs.
    - `tshark` finds 18 distinct source addresses behind it.
    - They run two stacks.
    - The stacks need different configuration, NAT handling and re-INVITE handling.
  - The new `stack` block reports the OBSERVATION:
    - `branch_cookie`, `branch_shape`, `tag_shape`, `callid_has_host`.
  - `inference` and `confidence` derive from it.
  - `requests_read` is the denominator.
  - The inference names a LIBRARY, never a product.
    - `z9hG4bKPj` is pjproject's.
    - pjproject ships inside Asterisk's `res_pjsip`, Grandstream UCM and FreePBX alike.
  - `mixed` says when one address's own requests disagree.

    - That is what a shared address or a relaying proxy looks like.
  - It reads from requests only.
    - A response echoes the request's branch, tag and Call-ID verbatim.
    - Reading one would fingerprint the caller as though it were the answerer.
  - Measured rather than assumed.
    - The branch suffix is 8, 9 **and** 10 hex digits in the corpus.
    - A rule pinned to one length would have missed most of them.

## [0.5.159] - 2026-09-08

### Added

- **Why a call ended, as a field.**
  - These surfaces now carry a `termination` block:
    - `triage_call`
    - `get_dialog_report`
    - `GET /v1/dialogs/{call_id}/report`
    - `--call-report`
  - The block has `cause_code`, `cause_text`, `protocol`, `source_header` and `frame_ref`.
  - "The call ended" and "the call ended because the far end was out of order"
    are different answers.
    - Only the second closes a ticket.
  - sipnab already parsed [RFC 3326](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3326.html) `Reason`.
    - It read it in exactly one place: the final failure response.
    - A normally-cleared call never reaches that response.
  - A `Reason` on a `BYE` or a `CANCEL` now counts.
    - sipnab reads it from the last message that names a cause.
  - `protocol` is carried because a cause code without its scale is not interpretable.
    - 16 is normal clearing in Q.850.
    - It is not a SIP status code at all.
  - Where a message carries both, the non-`SIP` value wins.
    - `SIP;cause=` restates `final_status_code`, which is already its own field.
  - sipnab reads Asterisk's `X-Asterisk-HangupCauseCode` and `X-Asterisk-HangupCause` as one cause.
    - `source_header` says which header asserted the value.

  - **The generic half is the feature; the vendor half is two header names.**
  - `termination` is a fact, not a fault.
    - It sits beside `verdict` and never moves it.
    - A call that cleared normally reports `verdict: "none"` and a cause at the same time.
    - Both are true.

- **Every header the per-message projection left behind.**
  - `get_message`, `get_dialog`, `--json` and `-N --json` now carry `extension_headers`.
    - It holds every header outside the closed field list.
    - Each is in wire form (`"Name: value"`) and in wire order.
  - The projection had `from`, `to`, `contact`, `ua`, `cseq`, `call_id` and nothing else.
  - So every vendor-, carrier- and SBC-specific fact reached no surface at all.
    - Examples: `X-Asterisk-*`, `Reason`, `Diversion`, `P-Asserted-Identity`,
      `Remote-Party-ID`, `Require`, `RSeq`.
  - The parser had always retained them.
    - This was a projection gap, not a parsing one.
  - Duplicates and order are preserved.
    - `Via` is a stack whose order is the route the request took.
  - Each entry is fenced whole, name included.
    - For an extension header, the name is as much the sender's choice as the value.
  - `deferred-and-declined.md` said `get_message` returned "headers and body included".
    - That was false when written.
    - It now says so, and says which release made it true.

- **`${NAME}` in config values.**
  - Any string in `sipnab.toml` may name an environment variable.
  - sipnab expands it when it reads the file.
  - The case it exists for is `sudo`.
    - After `sudo -i`, a file written by the run lands in root's directory.
    - It does not land in the directory of whoever ran the command.
    - `${SUDO_USER}` is the only thing that can say which one that is.
  - An unset variable is an **error**, not an empty expansion.
    - `/home/${SUDO_USER}/sipnab` with nothing set becomes `/home//sipnab`.
    - That is a real and writable directory that is not the one anybody meant.
  - `$$` is a literal `$` everywhere, not only before a brace.
  - A bare `$NAME` stays literal.
  - sipnab never rescans what a variable expands to.

### Fixed

- **Four tests read the wrong repository under `git commit`.**
  - The staged-inputs gate's fixtures scrub `GIT_DIR` and `GIT_INDEX_FILE`
    from the child `git` they drive.
  - They did not scrub them from the child `python3` that runs the script under test.
    - That script shells out to a git of its own.
    - It handed the variables straight on.
  - Under a real commit, those four tests reported on the repository being
    committed to rather than on their fixture.
  - They passed whenever someone ran the hook by hand, where the variables are unset.
    - So the failure only ever appeared at the moment of committing.
  - One list now serves both children.
  - A test compares the two as sets.

- **Three doc blocks were split by an item inserted between them and what they
  documented.**
  - `CidrRange::contains` shipped in 0.5.158 documented, in full, as `they asked for.`.
    - The four paragraphs explaining the IPv4-mapped rule had been left on `network_addr`.
    - That item was inserted into the middle of them.
  - `run_mint_token` and `ACCUSED_FINDING_SCAN_CAP` carried the same defect.
  - Nothing failed.
    - Each block still compiled and still sat on an item.
  - A new gate reads where a block BEGINS rather than what it contains.
    - That is the half a split leaves evidence in.
    - The second item always inherits a fragment.
    - A fragment opens with a pronoun, article or preposition.
  - It found all three on its first run.

- **A recorded call's report failed schema validation outright.**
  - `call_report.schema.json` says `additionalProperties: false`.
  - It had never declared `siprec`.
    - `--call-report --json` and `GET /v1/dialogs/{call_id}/report` have
      emitted it for every SIPREC call since the field shipped.
  - A consumer validating sipnab's output rejected the whole report.
  - A new census found it.
    - It compares the Rust projection's fields against the published schema in both directions.
  - The existing schema tests validate sample output.
    - So a field no fixture carries could stay undeclared indefinitely.
    - A schema entry for a field the code stopped emitting could sit there forever.
    - It would tell a consumer to expect something that never arrives.

- **A redacted vCon published the operator's proxy chain by name.**

  - `Path`, `Route`, `Record-Route` and `Service-Route` were all on the
    redactor's host-bearing list.
  - `Via`, the one header every SIP message carries, was not.
    - [RFC 3261 section 20.42](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3261.html#section-20.42) gives it `sent-protocol SP
  sent-by`, not a name-addr.
    - So it did not fit beside them.
    - It fell through to the free-text sweep.
    - The sweep finds addresses and numbers and walks straight past a hostname.
  - Its `received` and `maddr` parameters go through the same rule now.
  - `branch` is kept.
    - It is the transaction handle a reader follows.
    - Tokenizing it would cost the correlation and hide nothing.
  - The existing leak test could not have caught this.
    - Its fixture carries eleven identifying headers and no `Via`.

- **A credential written as a wire line walked through the export filter.**
  - `strip_credentials` removed JSON object entries whose KEY was `Authorization`.
    - That is the shape the vCon header map has.
  - It now also filters a string that IS a header line.
    - It keys on the name before the colon.
  - So the publication boundary holds for the shape a field arrives in.
    - It no longer depends on the shape a field had when the filter was written.

- **The E-model's loss term had an unguarded pole.**
  - `estimate_r_with_delay` checked `jitter_ms` and `one_way_delay_ms` for
    finite and non-negative.
  - It did not check `loss_pct`.
    - Its G.107 Appendix I term divides by `Ppl + 10`.
  - At `Ppl = -10` exactly:
    - The term went to negative infinity.
    - The subtraction went to positive infinity.
    - The existing clamp handed back a perfect **100.0**.
    - That is finite, on the scale, and the best score the function can return.
  - A NaN reached the MOS against a documented `[1.0, 4.5]`.
  - The wideband model had the same defect by another route.
    - `ie_eff_wb` guards `loss_pct <= 0.0`, which is false for a NaN.
  - One admissible range now serves both.

- **Two more Mermaid generators, neither capped.**
  - `src/wasm.rs` and the TUI call-flow export each built a `sequenceDiagram` themselves.
    - They did not go through `src/mermaid.rs`.
  - The browser one mattered.
    - The vendored renderer refuses a diagram over `maxEdges: 500` outright.
    - So a long SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY dialog rendered as nothing at all.
  - Both now go through one generator. It does three things:
    - It caps.
    - It declares every participant.
    - It carries the annotations the ladder had already computed as `Note` lines.
      - Timestamps, PDD, SDP direction, retransmission and folded counts.
  - IPv6 participants are bracketed.
    - So two endpoints differing only in port can no longer merge into one lifeline.

- **The WASM plugin ABI documented four exports where the host resolves
  three.**

  - The host never called `sipnab_dealloc`.
  - The docs now name what the host actually looks up.
  - A test compares the two sets.
    - It does not merely check that each name appears somewhere.

### Changed

- **41 British spellings inside identifiers, across 44 files.**
  - The US-English gate reads prose.
  - Identifiers were invisible to it and had drifted.
  - `--uprobe-flavour` survives as a deliberate alias, because it is a released flag.
  - The `flavours` MCP wire key also survives.
    - clap errors loudly on an unknown flag.
    - serde ignores an unknown key in silence.

## [0.5.158] - 2026-09-08

### Fixed

- **`in_subnet` refused addresses the HEP allowlist accepts.**
  - `--hep-allow 198.51.100.0/24` admits an agent whose packets arrive as `::ffff:198.51.100.7`.
    - [RFC 4291 section 2.5.5.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4291.html#section-2.5.5.2)
      makes `::ffff:0:0/96` the representation *of* an IPv4 address.
    - It is not a different family.
    - The allowlist maps it accordingly.
  - The filter DSL had its own CIDR rule and refused the same address.
    - So `src.ip in_subnet '198.51.100.0/24'` selected none of the traffic that
      prefix had just admitted.
  - The uprobe backend produces exactly this shape.
    - It reads `sk_v6_rcv_saddr` verbatim for any `AF_INET6` socket.
    - So a proxy bound to `[::]` yields mapped addresses with no canonicalization in between.
  - The two also disagreed about a bare address.
    - `198.51.100.40` is a host route on the allowlist.
    - It matched nothing in a filter.
  - `CidrRange` moved out of the `hep`-gated module into `crate::net`.
  - The DSL uses it.

- **The load-bearing verdict could not see the limit it was measuring
  against.**
  - `host_stats` read `/sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max` and nothing else.

    - That finds a limit only for a process in the cgroup-v2 root.
    - The v2 root carries no controller files.
    - So on an ordinary systemd host it finds nothing at all.
  - These were invisible:
    - A unit with `MemoryMax=`.
    - Every container.
    - Every cgroup-v1 system.
  - Example: sipnab at 1.5 GiB inside a 2 GiB cap.
    - It reported 1.2% of a 128 GiB machine and `significant: false`.
    - It was about to be OOM-killed at the time.
    - That is precisely the question that field exists to answer.
  - The probe now resolves this process's own cgroup.
    - It walks to the root, taking the tightest limit.
    - Limits are hierarchical, and a slice's cap binds every unit inside it.
    - It then falls back to v1.
      - There, "unlimited" is a sentinel rather than a keyword.
  - `memory_available_bytes` comes from the same limit now.
    - It used to stay on `/proc/meminfo`.
    - That file is not namespaced without lxcfs.
    - So a container with a 1 GiB cap on a 128 GiB host reported 1 GiB total
      and ~100 GiB available.
    - Those were two numbers from two different machines, printed as a pair.
  - The subtraction happens where the limit is read.
    - So no caller can pair them wrongly again.

- **Eight places where one rule was written twice.**
  - An audit of the tree found them.
    - It looked for the class that produced the `P-Charging-Vector` leak.
  - Two were already wrong in production.
  - **The two scrape doors published different data.**
    - `--api /metrics` lowercased the dialog-state label.
    - The standalone `--metrics` server did not.
    - So one deployment served `state="completed"` on one port and
      `state="Completed"` on the other.
    - The dashboards in `contrib/` query the lowercase form.
      - So their "Active Dialogs" panel read empty against the standalone server.
      - That is indistinguishable from an idle switch.
    - Five more differences traveled with it:
      - `sipnab_rtp_streams_active` counted two different populations under one name.
      - `sipnab_rtp_streams_total` existed on only one door.
      - Both dialog gauges were missing from one.
      - All four quality histograms were missing from one.
      - The capture-queue counters read a flat `0` on the other.
    - `docs/prometheus-metrics.md` listed all six as permanent.
    - There is now one assembler.
    - `both_scrape_doors_publish_identical_exposition` compares the formatted
      exposition the two produce for one capture.

  - **The shipped alert rules paged on conformant traffic.**
    - `contrib/prometheus/sipnab-alerts.yml` fired at PDD > 5 s.
    - The code calls a call healthy until 11 s.
    - 5.0 s is ITU-T E.721 (05/99) Table 2's toll normal-load *mean* target.
      - A toll route sitting there is meeting the standard.
    - Both tiers are now grounded in that table, read from the recommendation itself:
      - Warn at 6.0 s (local connection, normal load, 95%).
        - Twilio's Voice Insights documentation independently names this as
          the US carrier-escalation line.

      - Page at 11.0 s (international, normal load, 95%).
        - This is the same figure `SignalingThresholds::BUILT_IN` uses.
    - A test fails the build if the two ever disagree, in both copies of the file.
  - **`is_unconfigured` was answered twice.**

    - One copy gates the REST per-request auth bypass.
    - The other gates the MCP bind refusal.
    - Someone could add a third credential source to one and not the other.
      - That would have allowed a non-loopback bind.
      - Every request would still short-circuit to `Ok(())`.
    - There is one predicate now.
    - A test drives all four credential shapes through both.
  - **REST carried a private rate limiter.**

    - So `[limits] max_tracked_peers` was inert there.
    - Its bucket map had no configured bound against a spoofed-source flood.
    - It now uses the shared `FixedWindowLimiter`.
    - A separate gate covers the wiring, apart from the limiter.
      - Testing the limiter proved the limiter worked.
      - It said nothing about whether the configured numbers reached it.
      - That was the half that was broken.
  - **The shipped fail2ban filter was ungated.**
    - It pins the field order of the log lines sipnab writes.
    - A filter that stops matching fails silently.
      - The jail keeps running and bans nothing.
      - That looks exactly like a quiet network.
    - It is now compiled against real log lines.
    - A decoy test stops it passing by being a catch-all.
  - **`DialogState` spellings were written five times.**
    - The compiler caught an added variant in all five.
    - It caught a changed spelling in none.
    - None of them asserted `Redirected`.
    - So renaming it in the filter DSL alone would have left
      `--filter "state == 'Redirected'"` silently returning zero rows.
    - There is one table now, driven by `DialogState::ALL`.
  - **The starter config named a path sipnab never reads.**
    - `contrib/sipnabrc.example` advertised `./sipnab.toml` first.
    - It omitted `/etc/sipnab/sipnab.toml`.
    - So a reader following it copied the file where sipnab would not look.
    - The loader is lenient, so nothing said so.
  - **And three smaller pairs:**
    - `MosGrounding::is_grounded()` is a single definition.
      - It was one copy each in the REST and MCP projections.

    - `RttSource::as_wire_str()` is a single definition in the same way.
    - `limit=0` now means the default page on every REST route.
      - It always did on MCP.
      - It previously meant an empty page on two of them.
      - So a caller who interpolated an unset variable into a URL got a
        successful response with no rows.
      - That read as "there is nothing here" rather than as a mistake.

## [0.5.157] - 2026-09-07

### Fixed

- **`pre-push` now runs the E2E TUI tests, which ran nowhere else locally.**
  - They drive a real sipnab in a real PTY through tmux.
  - They are the only check that a key does what a user pressing it would see.
  - They are `#[ignore]`d, so `cargo test` skips them.
    - The pre-commit suite, the feature matrix and every local run passed without them.
  - The quit confirmation below broke `tui_quit_exits_cleanly`.
    - That test pressed `q` and waited for the process to end.
    - Nothing local could have caught it.
  - When tmux is absent, they are skipped with a stated verdict, never silently.

- **The US-English gate had a hole in it, and the spelling came back through
  the hole.**
  - Its word list left out `neighbour` entirely.
    - So `neighbours` reached a released changelog entry.
  - `flavour` was deliberately excluded.
    - `--uprobe-flavour` is an accepted alias.
    - The gate could only exempt whole files.
  - Both are fixed the same way.
    - The list now carries the full families:
      - `neighbour`, `favour`, `defence`, `centre`, `labour`, `realise`,
        `utilise` and the rest.
    - The two legitimate British spellings are exempted by TOKEN rather than by file:
      - The flag name `uprobe-flavour`.
      - The serde attribute `alias = "flavours"` on the MCP `start_tls_capture` params.
    - The word stays forbidden in prose everywhere.

      - That includes the files those two tokens live in.
  - It found 35 occurrences across the tree.
    - Nearly all of them are older than this release.
  - `--uprobe-flavour` and the MCP `flavours` key both keep working.
    - A released flag and a wire field are contracts, not spelling choices.

### Added

- **A confirmation before quitting the TUI.**
  - `Esc` ended the session outright.
  - In every other view in sipnab, `Esc` means "go back".
  - In the call list it meant "go away".
    - A capture that has been running for an hour does not survive the difference.

  - `Esc` and the quit key now open a "Quit sipnab?" dialog:
    - `Y` or Enter quits.
    - `N`/`Esc`/`q` returns to the session.
    - Any other key leaves the question standing rather than dismissing it.
  - `Ctrl-C` still quits immediately.
    - It works while the dialog is open.
    - The popup handler runs before the view handlers.
    - Otherwise a confirmation nobody could dismiss would have trapped the terminal.
    - That is the one gesture nobody presses by accident.
  - Seven views each set `should_quit` themselves.
    - They now route through one `request_quit`.
    - So the answer to "should this really exit?" lives in one place rather than seven.
  - Reported by liwangob ([@WangKLi](https://github.com/WangKLi)) (#283).
    - They pointed out that `Esc` is the key a terminal user presses
      reflexively to back out of something.
    - That makes it the worst possible key to end a session with.

## [0.5.156] - 2026-09-07

### Added

- **`runtime_stats` over MCP and `GET /v1/runtime` over REST.**
  - sipnab exports 32 Prometheus metrics.
  - The listener that serves them is off by default.
  - So on most deployments those numbers existed inside the process and nothing could read them.
    - An agent asked "is this server healthy" could not enable a listener to find out.
  - Two things here did not exist anywhere:
    - sipnab could not state its own resident set size, virtual size, thread
      count, descriptor count or CPU time.
    - It could not say what fraction of the host it was using.
  - A capture that is itself the reason a proxy started dropping calls is the
    worst failure this tool can have.
    - It was invisible.

  - **The host figures name their basis.**
    - Inside a container, the real denominators are the control group's limits,
      not the machine's.
    - So the answer says `cgroup` and reads `memory.max`.
    - A percentage computed against the wrong total is worse than no percentage.
      - A reader believes it.
  - **`impact.significant` is a verdict, not arithmetic.**
    - The threshold is stated.
    - So you can disagree with the setting rather than the finding.
  - An absent field means "not readable on this platform", never zero.

- **Interface statistics, read from the interface rather than the capture
  handle.**
  - sipnab's own `ps_recv`/`ps_drop`/`ps_ifdrop` describe what reached sipnab.
  - `/sys/class/net` describes what reached the NIC.
  - The pair is what separates the two remedies:
    - `ps_ifdrop` climbing with `rx_missed_errors` is hardware that cannot keep up.
      - The fix is ring size, coalescing or RSS.
    - `ps_drop` climbing alone is sipnab's read loop falling behind.
      - The fix is `--buffer` or a tighter filter.
  - The handle counter alone cannot tell them apart.

- **Store occupancy against the caps.**
  - `dialogs.used` alone is a number.
  - Beside `capacity` it is a decision.
  - An operator who cannot see occupancy learns about eviction by noticing
    that calls have gone missing.

- **Rates, opt-in via `sample_seconds`, broken down by method.**
  - Every counter above is cumulative.
  - A cumulative total answers a different question from a rate.
  - The breakdown is the point.
    - A rate that does not separate INVITE from OPTIONS describes whatever the
      deployment does most.
    - In the field, that is the keepalive plane rather than the calls.
  - It is opt-in rather than defaulted.
    - The measurement costs a wait of exactly the window asked for.
    - Every other field answers instantly.
  - The reply carries the window that was **applied**, not the one requested.
  - One function refuses zero and clamps long windows for both surfaces.
  - REST narrows it further to what it can answer inside its own request timeout.
    - So no window one surface accepts is one the other kills mid-sleep.

- **The E-model R-factor is published.**
  - sipnab computed `R = R0 - Is - Id - Ie_eff + A` on every stream.
  - It returned only the MOS it converts to.
  - Carriers write thresholds and SLAs in R.
  - R is the linear scale.

    - Eight R-points is a real difference.
    - The MOS gap it maps to looks like rounding.
  - It carries the same grounding flags as the MOS, because it is the same derivation.
    - `estimate_mos_with_delay` is now `r_to_mos` of `estimate_r_with_delay`.
    - So the two scales cannot disagree about one stream.

- **`in_subnet`, a filter operator that compares addresses rather than
  strings.**
  - The only subnet answer the DSL had was a regex on the dotted form.
  - That has three problems:
    - It cannot express a prefix which is not octet-aligned.
      - A `/22` spans four `/24`s.
    - It matches neighbors when the anchor is dropped.
    - IPv6 defeats it entirely.
      - `2001:db8::1` and its fully expanded form are one address and two strings.
  - Malformed input now matches nothing rather than everything.
  - The two families never cross.

### Fixed

- **The documented Prometheus metric count was wrong, and nothing held it.**
  - One backlog line claimed sipnab exports 42 metric families.
  - The exposition emits 32.
  - Nothing gated the figure.
  - So it propagated before anyone measured it, into:
    - A changelog entry.
    - Two operator pages.
    - A tool description.
    - A module doc.
  - `prose_metric_counts_match_the_exposition` now reads every surface that states a count.
    - It checks them against the same scan the documentation-drift gate uses.
    - So adding a metric moves the number rather than quietly invalidating six sentences.

- **`--redact` leaked the real URI when a display name ended in an escaped
  quote.**

  - [RFC 3261 section 25.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3261.html#section-25.1)
    lets `quoted-pair` escape the closing DQUOTE.
    - So `\"` does not end a quoted string.
  - `split_top_level_commas` honored that.
  - `name_addr_one` scanned for the first bare `"` and did not.
  - A sender who closes the quote early moved every following byte past the rewriter.
    - The display name is theirs to choose.

  - `From`/`To`/`Contact` emerged from a container the tool calls redacted.
    - They carried a real E.164 number in clear.
    - They carried the operator's own hostname in clear.
  - There was no backstop.
    - `header()` returns `HeaderAction::Replace`.
    - The free-text sweep runs only for `Keep`.
  - The same file's `header_params` and `uri_params` split on every `;`.
    - That includes ones inside a quoted value.
    - So a `+sip.instance` or `maddr` carrying one was torn in half.
    - Its tail was emitted verbatim.
  - All three now go through one scanner.
  - Two of the three copies were wrong.
    - That is the argument against having had three.

- **`calls_per_second` measured store occupancy, not calls.**
  - The rate was built from `DialogStore::len()`.
    - That is how many dialogs are HELD.
  - At the store's cap, that number is pinned while calls arrive and leave.

    - So the headline rate of this release answered `0.0/s` on exactly the
      saturated server an operator was asking about.
  - Below the cap, it canceled to zero whenever completions matched arrivals.
  - The store now carries a cumulative opened-per-method counter.
  - The total is its sum.
    - It is not a second counter that could drift from it.
  - A method whose dialogs have all gone keeps its row.
    - So a fall to zero reads as a fall rather than as a disappearance.

- **The capture queue depth and backpressure count were hardcoded zero on both
  new surfaces.**
  - `runtime_stats` and `GET /v1/runtime` both passed `None` for the meter.
  - Both fields were `u64`.
  - So a saturated pipeline reported `capture_queue_depth_packets: 0`.
    - That reads as "the queue is clear".
    - `/metrics` on the same process reported the truth.
  - The meter now reaches both doors from the same place the scrape endpoint gets it.
  - The two fields are optional.
    - They are absent where no meter is held, never zero.
  - `batch.rs` already carried a comment describing this exact trap one layer down.

- **The published OpenAPI schema for `GET /v1/runtime` omitted `rates`.**
  - `schema::Runtime` is a hand-written mirror with no `Serialize`.
  - So nothing compared it to the type the route actually sends.
  - A generated client dropped the field the route's own description tells callers to ask for.
  - `the_runtime_schema_names_every_field_the_route_sends` now compares the two
    in both directions.
