- **A capture-channel test measured the OS scheduler rather than the meter.**
  - `instant_recovery_cap_hit_is_not_a_genuine_block` raced two threads for 10,000 iterations.
  - It asserted a ratio between genuine blocks and raw capacity hits.
  - It failed the macOS runner twice while the code was correct.
    - Once at 0.5.122, and once here.

  - Whether a fall-back send returns within the same instant depends on
    whether the consumer thread happens to be on a core.
  - The rule it was reaching for is a comparison against a 1 ms threshold.
    - There is no scheduler in it.
  - So that rule is now a function, and the tests drive it directly:
    - At zero.
    - Just under the threshold.
    - At it.
    - Past it.
  - The end-to-end test keeps only what a scheduler cannot change.

- **`render_ladder` returned tables.**
  - The tool named for a ladder produced a call report.
  - Its own description said so.
  - It now emits a Mermaid `sequenceDiagram` with:
    - `autonumber`.
    - Positional participant ids, so no capture-derived text reaches an identifier.
    - A message cap that states the truncation inside the diagram.
      - It does not leave a picture that quietly omits half the call.

## [0.5.155] - 2026-09-06

### Fixed

- **`--redact` returned everything after the first comma verbatim.**
  - Every header in the identity and routing families is `value *(COMMA value)`.
    - See [RFC 3325 section 9.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3325.html#section-9.1),
      [RFC 3327 section 4](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3327.html#section-4),
      [RFC 7044 section 5](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7044.html#section-5),
      [RFC 3261 section 20.10](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3261.html#section-20.10) and
      [RFC 3261 section 20.30](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3261.html#section-20.30).
  - A two-value `P-Asserted-Identity` is the ordinary IMS shape.
  - It came out of a container the tool calls redacted, carrying:
    - A real E.164 subscriber number.
    - A display name.
    - The operator's own core hostnames.
  - Splitting is now quote and bracket aware.

    - [RFC 3261 section 25.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3261.html#section-25.1)
      puts `,` inside `qdtext`.

- **The redactor had a second `P-Charging-Vector` parser beside the correct
  one.**
  - It tore `icid-value="aaa;SECRET"` in half and emitted the tail in clear.
  - It now uses the shared walker.
  - A quoted value preceded by legal whitespace also lost its mandatory quotes.

- **A conformant `m=video 49170/2` fabricated facts about another stream.**
  - [RFC 8866 section 5.14](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8866.html#section-5.14)'s
    port-count form failed to parse.
  - The parser stayed "in media".
  - So every following attribute landed on the previous section.
  - The result was an audio stream that:
    - Reported as sendonly.
    - Was anchored to the video's address.
    - Carried the video's codec.

- **Session-level SDP direction attributes were dropped.**
  - That silently disarmed a lint rule.
  - The same [RFC 3264 section 6.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3264.html#section-6.1)
    violation fired when written at media level and not at session level.
  - [RFC 8866 section 6.7](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8866.html#section-6.7)
    makes the session-level value the default for any media description that declares none.

- **A `Contact` URI parameter was read as the binding lifetime.**
  - `<sip:alice@host;expires=60>;expires=3600` reported "Registration granted 60s
    against 3600s requested".
  - Everything inside the angle brackets is URI parameters
    ([RFC 3261 section 25.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3261.html#section-25.1)).
  - [section 10.2.1.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3261.html#section-10.2.1.1)
    puts the lifetime on the header parameter.

- **A caller could choose the dialog identifier.**
  - `extract_tag` anchored on the first `>` in the raw value.
  - So a display name of `"A>;tag=decoy"` supplied the From tag.
    - That is half the dialog ID under
      [RFC 3261 section 12.1.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3261.html#section-12.1.1).
  - It also missed `; tag = x` and `;TAG=`, both conformant.

- **A response with an empty Reason-Phrase was discarded.**
  - [RFC 4475 section 3.1.1.13](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4475.html#section-3.1.1.13):
    "A parser must accept this message."
  - `line.trim()` destroyed the required trailing space.
  - The whole response vanished with only a debug line.

- **A comma-combined `Via` returned a later hop's branch.**
  - Everything keyed on the transaction read that:
    - Retransmission detection.
    - Scanner and registration-flood detection.
    - Digest-leak detection.
    - Three lint rules.

- **`Session-ID` was remotely spoofable.**

  - The `remote` parameter name was matched case-sensitively.
  - Parameters were split without quote awareness.
  - So one appended `generic-param` overwrote the genuine remote half.
    - That killed B2BUA correlation silently.
  - A duplicate now takes the first, per
    [RFC 7989 section 5](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7989.html#section-5).

- **Only the first `Identity` header was read.**
  - [RFC 8224 section 4](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8224.html#section-4) permits more than one.
  - An [RFC 8946](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8946.html) diverted call carries two.
  - The second PASSporT was invisible everywhere.
  - An unparseable token was logged at debug and nowhere else.
    - It is now a warning and is carried in the result.

- **[RFC 3611 section 4.7](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3611.html#section-4.7)
  jitter-buffer fields were read two octets early.**
  - `jb_nominal` held the RX-config bits.
  - Each later field held its predecessor's value.
  - JB abs max was never read at all.
  - The 65535 ceiling was tested against the wrong field.
  - The existing test built its fixture in the parser's order.
    - It called the shortfall "2 bytes padding".
  - The [RFC 3611 section 4.7](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3611.html#section-4.7)
    body is 32 octets of defined fields.

- **[RFC 3550 section 5.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3550.html#section-5.1)
  padding was decoded and never stripped.**
  - So padding octets were counted into the reported bitrate.
  - They were also exported as audio samples.

- **A truncated RTCP packet became a phantom RTP stream.**
  - Only types 200-204 were rejected.
  - So a snaplen-truncated XR (207) fell through.
  - Its block header was reported as an SSRC.
  - [RFC 3551 section 6](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3551.html#section-6)
    leaves payload types 64-95 unassigned.
    - The purpose is that RTCP types 192-223 stay distinguishable.

- **Every DTMF keypress was counted three times.**

  - [RFC 4733 section 2.5.1.4](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4733.html#section-2.5.1.4)
    requires the final packet be sent three times with the E bit set.
  - The retransmissions share SSRC, RTP timestamp and event code.
  - That is now the dedupe key.

- **A STUN message reported a bad fingerprint because of trailing octets.**
  - `attr_start` was measured against the datagram rather than the message.
  - Duplicate attributes took the last.
    - [RFC 8489 section 14](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8489.html#section-14) says the first.
  - MESSAGE-INTEGRITY covers only what precedes it.

- **TURN channel numbers used [RFC 5766](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5766.html)'s range.**

  - [RFC 8656](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8656.html) Table 3 reserves `0x5000-0xFFFF`.
  - Narrowing also quarters the accidental-match rate.
  - That rate is what previously let GTPv2-C control messages be unwrapped as relayed media.

- **GTPv2-C control traffic was reported as an RTP stream with a confident
  MOS.**
  - A ChannelData header and a GTPv2-C header are the same shape.
  - Both define Length identically.
  - So only the port can separate them.

- **The browser analyzer's Mermaid export escaped nothing.**
  - It interpolated the sender-written reason phrase straight into diagram source.
  - The escaper now lives in one ungated module both targets reach.
  - It gained `%`.
    - `%%` opens a Mermaid comment and silently truncated a label.

- **`security.fraud_destination` and `theme.status_bg` warned on every start.**
  - Both are real fields read by working code.
  - Neither was registered.
  - So setting them worked and logged `Unknown config key`.

- **437's reason phrase was superseded.**
  - [RFC 8224 section 6.2.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8224.html#section-6.2.2)
    renamed it to Unsupported Credential.

### Added

- **Three tests pinning each media asymmetry to the leg it was measured on.**
  - `collect_media` has four arms of one `if let` chain.
  - Each pulls two fields off a struct whose members differ only by an `a_`/`b_` prefix.
  - That is the shape a copy-paste swap survives.
    - The finding still appears with both numbers present.
    - An operator reads the A leg's packetization as the B leg's.
  - Distinct values per leg make a swap visible.
  - Swapping either pair now turns a test red.
  - A negative late-media delay is also pinned.
    - It clamps to zero.
    - It does not wrap through the cast into billions of milliseconds.

### Fixed

- **An empty inline secret authenticated any peer that presented an empty
  one.**
  - `--hep-auth ""` resolved to `Some("")`.
  - That is worse than no secret at all.
    - It satisfies the SN-01 bind policy.
    - So a non-loopback listener is permitted on the strength of
      "authentication is configured".
    - Then the constant-time comparison finds an empty expected value equal to
      an empty presented one.

  - The operator believes the listener is guarded.
  - It admits whoever asks.
  - The file path had always refused this.
    - An empty or whitespace-only file is a hard error naming the flag.
  - The inline path passed its value through untouched.
    - So the same bytes were fatal from one source and a valid secret from the other.
  - Both are one rule now.
  - Inline values are trimmed to match, too.
    - Moving a secret off the command line into a file is the documented advice.
    - The file's contents are trimmed.
    - Without this, following that advice changed the secret.
    - The symptom is every agent failing auth at once with nothing to point at.
  - The resolver is shared.
    - So `--metrics-auth` had the same hole and the same fix.

## [0.5.154] - 2026-09-06

### Fixed

- **A HEP allowlist refused every legitimate agent reaching a dual-stack
  listener.**
  - `--hep-listen [::]:9060` accepts IPv4 connections.
  - Linux reports those peers as `::ffff:a.b.c.d`.
  - `CidrRange::contains` treated any IPv6 address as a family mismatch against an IPv4 range.
  - So `--hep-allow 198.51.100.0/24` matched nothing at all.
  - That is the strict direction, but it does not end safely.
    - Operators widen or switch off an allowlist that refuses everyone.
    - SN-01 pushes operators toward exactly this pairing.
    - It requires an allowlist or auth for any non-loopback bind.
    - The failure is silent from the operator's side: agents simply never appear.
  - An IPv4-mapped address now matches an IPv4 range.

    - The reason: the operator named a host rather than a socket family.
    - A range written in the mapped form stays IPv6 and keeps matching as one.

  - Found by writing a test for the case rather than for the code.
  - Two companion tests drive every IPv4 and IPv6 prefix length -- 161 of them.
    - Each runs against the network address of the range it builds.
    - The reason: the code computes the prefix mask in two places.
    - Two copies of one rule on an allowlist is how a host nobody named gets admitted.
    - Those two tests passed, so the duplication is at least consistent today.

### Added

- **The coverage floor moves 92 to 93, and there is a way to check it before
  pushing.**
  - Line coverage measured 93.64% (128472/137200).
  - Functions measured 94.19% and regions 93.90%.
  - The workflow's own comment says to raise the floor when the real number rises.
  - So the floor is raised.
    - The measurement and the commit it came from are recorded beside it.
  - `scripts/coverage.sh` reproduces the CI coverage job locally.
    - It reads the floor and the two `--skip` flags out of `quality.yml` rather than repeating them.
    - Two copies of a threshold is how a gate and its local rehearsal come to disagree.
    - The rehearsal is the one that gets trusted, because it answers first.
  - `tests/coverage_gate_test.rs` fails in three cases:
    - The script grows its own floor.
    - The two skip different tests.
    - The floor is walked backwards.
  - It is deliberately not in the pre-push hook, and a test asserts it stays out.
    - An instrumented build plus the full suite is 30-60 minutes.
    - The hook already takes around fifteen.
    - People bypass a gate nobody waits for.

### Fixed

- **The Dependabot note now covers the case that actually broke `main`.**
  - `docs/internals/build-ci-release.md` already said every Dependabot pull
    request fails on the generated third-party notices.
  - It gave the one command that fixes it on a branch.
  - It did not say what happens when five are merged together.
    - Regenerating on one branch does not help the four merged after it.
    - The reason: each merge changes the graph again.
  - The shape that works: merge the batch, then regenerate once at the end, on `main`.

## [0.5.153] - 2026-09-06

### Fixed

- **A `<send>` list could lose every entry after an empty one, and a
  self-closing entry could report markup as a stream id.**
  - Both are in `extract_all_xml_content`, which resolves SIPREC stream ownership.
  - Both came in with that feature earlier in this release cycle.
  - The scan called the single-value reader in a loop.
    - That reader answers `None` for an element with no content.
    - The loop read `None` as "no more".
    - So one `<send></send>` anywhere in a participant's list silently discarded every stream after it.
    - The participant then owned fewer streams than the SRC said.
    - That is worse than owning none: the answer looks plausible with a stream missing from it.
  - Worse, the loop advanced by searching for the next closing tag from the start of the remainder.
    - A self-closing `<send/>` has no closing tag.
    - So it consumed the following element's closing tag.
    - It returned the literal string `<send>s1` as a stream identifier.
  - The scan now walks the elements itself.
    - It skips empty and self-closing ones.
    - It continues rather than stops.
    - Neither kind names a stream.
    - Neither is a reason to stop reading the ones that do.
  - A third defect surfaced under mutation.
    - The guard that stops `<sendonly>` matching `<send>` had no test at all.
    - Removing it left every test green.
  - Found by writing tests intended to fail rather than tests intended to pass.
    - The fifteen tests added for coverage immediately before these found nothing.
    - These three found three defects in code written the same day.

## [0.5.152] - 2026-09-05

### Added

- **SIPREC reaches the CLI report, which was the surface it had missed.**
  - MCP, REST and the ladder carried it; `--call-report` did not.
  - That is the one an operator reads with no agent and no HTTP client.
  - The report now names:
    - The recording session and mode.
    - The participants.
    - Each stream's label, resolved to the party that sends it.
  - It resolves by AOR rather than the participant UUID.
    - Nobody can read a UUID off a screen.

- **A recipe for reading a recorded call, and HEP transport one-liners.**

  - Recipe "See who is on a recorded call" shows what `--call-report` prints for a SIPREC call.
  - It explains what the label and participant fields mean.
  - The HEP quick-reference gained the TCP and TLS forms.
    - Both sides have named their own transport since 0.5.150.
    - The section still showed only UDP.

- **Two notes.**
  - One on the SIPREC arc:
    - A parser with tests, and a field on the dialog.
    - A feature that was dead on every live capture.
    - The fault sat between the parser and the store.

  - One on two macOS-only test failures that were the same mistake twice.
    - Both encoded when a kernel reports a peer's disconnect.
    - They treated that timing as if it were the behavior under test.

### Fixed

- **The README described HEP as it was two releases ago.**
  - "send/receive Homer Encapsulation Protocol" has been wrong since 0.5.150.
  - That release added TCP and TLS on both sides.
  - The feature list said nothing about SIPREC at all.

### Added

- **Eighteen tests over the parts of the SIPREC work nothing was driving.**
  - The surfacing shipped with nine tests, all of them on paths that worked.
  - These cover what happens when the input is not the happy case.
  - The parser:
    - An assoc naming a stream the metadata never described owns nothing rather than inventing one.
    - A stream nobody claims stays unowned.
      - It is not handed to the only participant present.
    - Two assocs claiming one stream resolve in document order rather than arbitrarily.
    - A body delimited with bare LF still parses.
      - The XML reading must not be stricter than the framing already is.
    - A `multipart` content type with no boundary is an error rather than empty metadata.
    - The tests drive the all-occurrences reader directly.
      - It is the difference between a participant owning one stream and owning both.
  - The store:
    - It keeps metadata on the dialog-creating INVITE.
      - This is the defect this release fixed, now pinned.
    - A REFER on a creating message still records its target.
      - This guards the refactor that put SDP, REFER and SIPREC behind one function.
    - A later recording body replaces an earlier one.
      - An SRC re-sends when a party joins.
    - A `multipart/mixed` body that is not SIPREC leaves the field empty.
      - It does not report the call as recorded.
  - The surfaces:
    - They refuse an unknown Call-ID rather than answer `recorded: false`.
      - Those are different facts.
    - The answer says how much of the capture stands behind it, and which capture that was.
    - A recorded call is listed like any other over both MCP and HTTP.
      - SIPREC is a property of a call and not a separate kind of object.
    - The report endpoint carries the block as well as the raw object.
    - The ladder states a missing owner and an unnamed party rather than rendering either blank.


## [0.5.151] - 2026-09-05

### Added

- **SIPREC metadata reaches every surface: MCP, REST, the ladder and the JSON.**
  - It was parsed and stored on the dialog and read by nothing.
  - `siprec_metadata` is a new MCP tool.
    - It takes a `call_id`.
    - It returns the recording session and the mode.
    - It returns the participants with their AOR and display name.
    - It returns the recorded streams.
    - Each stream names the `m=` line it was cut from and the participant that sends it.
  - `GET /v1/dialogs/{id}` carries the same block, inherited rather than reprojected.
    - REST serves `dialog_to_json`, which is the point of having one definition.
  - The call-flow ladder annotates a SIPREC INVITE in place.
    - It names who is recorded and maps each label to its owner.
    - It does this unconditionally.
    - An operator who turned SDP display off has not asked to stop being told a call is being recorded.
  - A call with no SIPREC answers `recorded: false`.
    - The reason it gives refuses to overclaim.
    - sipnab reports what reached the capture point.
    - So a recorder signaling on a path it cannot see is indistinguishable from a call nobody recorded.
  - sipnab reads SIPREC and does not speak it.
    - Terminating a recording session -- acting as an SRC or an SRS -- would put it in the call path.
    - That is the opposite of what it says about itself in its own output.

### Fixed

- **SIPREC metadata on the INVITE that opens a dialog was dropped entirely.**
  - `DialogStore::process_message` has three arms that apply a message's derived state:
    - One for an existing dialog.
    - One that creates a dialog.
    - The replay a merge performs.
  - Two parsed SIPREC and the creating arm did not.
  - An SRC puts its metadata on exactly the INVITE that creates the dialog.
    - So on a live capture the field was never filled.
  - The parser worked, and its unit tests passed.
  - The feature was dead in production.
  - The rule is one function now, called from all three arms.
    - A rule written three times is a rule that will be written twice, and this is what that costs.
  - Found by driving a capture end to end rather than a fixture.

    - The unit tests could not see it, because they never went through the store.


### Fixed

- **SIPREC metadata could not be read from what a real SRC sends.**
  - sipnab has parsed [RFC 7866](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7866.html) `application/rs-metadata+xml` for a long time.
  - It parsed it against a hand-written fixture.

    - The fixture nests `<participant>` and `<stream>` inside `<session>`.
    - It has `<aor>` as a child element.
  - OpenSIPS's `siprec` module emits them differently.
    - This was read from `modules/siprec/siprec_body.c`, since the packets that matter are the ones a real SRC sends.
    - It emits them as siblings of `<session>`.
    - It makes `aor` an attribute of `<nameID>`.
  - Two fields were dead as a result.
  - The recording mode is `<datamode>`.
    - That is what [RFC 7866 section 7](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7866.html#section-7) defines and what OpenSIPS writes.
    - sipnab looked for `<mode>` and found nothing.
    - So `mode` was `None` on every recorded call.
  - Stream ownership was worse.
    - It is the reason to carry this metadata at all.
    - Nothing inside `<stream>` names a participant.
    - The association lives in `<participantstreamassoc>`, whose `participant_id` attribute names the participant.
    - Its `<send>` children name the streams that participant originates.
    - Its `<recv>` children name the ones it only hears.
    - sipnab looked inside the stream block.
    - So `participant_id` was `None` on every stream.
    - The one route from a recorded stream back to the person on it was closed.
  - Five tests now drive OpenSIPS's own output shape.

    - One has a participant sending audio and video, so the labels are `m=` line indices.
  - Mutation: each of these turns one test red:
    - Dropping `datamode`.
    - Ignoring the assoc.
    - Counting `<recv>` as ownership.
    - Reading only the first `<send>`.

### Added

- **SIPREC metadata reaches the JSON surface.**
  - It was parsed and stored on the dialog, and no surface read it.
    - Not JSON, not REST, not MCP, not the TUI.
  - To anyone outside this repository, a parser with no reader is indistinguishable from an absent feature.
  - `siprec` now appears on a recorded dialog's JSON.
  - It is omitted entirely on a call that is not recorded.


## [0.5.150] - 2026-09-04

### Added
- **The three reasons an RTP stream has no call are now testable, and
  tested.**
  - `reconcile_orphans` tells an operator why media could not be attached to a dialog.
  - There are three reasons:
    - A relay named the endpoint, but no captured dialog claims it.
    - An SDP body named it, but no dialog holds it.
    - Nothing named it at all.
  - The distinction is the value of the tool.
    - The first sends someone looking for missing signaling.
    - The last says the capture never saw an explanation.
  - A match buried in an async handler decided it.
    - Reaching that handler needs a server, a store and a live capture.
    - Nothing drove it.
  - The mapping is a free function now.
    - The reason is the same as for `classify` beside it.
    - The handler calls it rather than keeping a second copy.
    - A second copy would agree today and drift when a variant is added.
  - Two tests cover it:
    - One drives every arm.
    - One requires the three explanations to differ from each other.
      - Three identical sentences would satisfy the first test while telling a reader nothing.
- **A gate for public documentation that links to items rustdoc cannot
  reach.**
  - `capture_hep` is `pub`.
  - The transport documentation added with the TCP and TLS work linked two items it cannot reach:
    - `HepIngest` (private).
    - `hep_stream_frame` (`pub(crate)`).
  - rustdoc refuses that.
    - A rendered page would carry a link the reader cannot follow.
  - But rustdoc runs in the pre-push hook and in CI, not in pre-commit.
    - So the links passed a full green pre-commit run, including its own suite.
    - The push ten minutes later is what caught them.
  - The new gate reads `src/` directly.
    - For every `pub` item, an intra-doc link naming something declared non-public in the same file is an error.
  - It is deliberately narrower than rustdoc.
    - It never guesses at cross-module resolution.
    - rustdoc stays the authority.
    - It answers the common case in seconds instead of minutes.
    - It answers before the commit rather than after it.
  - The gate skips `#[doc(hidden)]` items.
    - rustdoc renders no page for them and resolves none of their links.
    - Only damage to documentation could satisfy a gate stricter than its own authority.
  - A third test asserts the pre-push hook still runs `cargo doc` with `-D warnings` and `--all-features`.
    - This gate is worth only as much as the check standing behind it.
- **HEP over TCP and TLS, on both sides.**
  - `--hep-send` opened a `UdpSocket` and `--hep-listen` bound one.
  - There was no other option.
  - Homer's own agents and collectors all offer TCP or TLS.
    - An operator whose Homer agent or collector spoke TCP or TLS could not interoperate with sipnab at all.
  - Each side now names its own transport:
    - `--hep-send-transport udp|tcp|tls`
    - `--hep-listen-transport udp|tcp|tls`
  - Both default to `udp`.
    - A run that names neither behaves exactly as it did.
  - There is deliberately no one flag covering both sides.
    - sipnab is both agent and collector, frequently in one process.
    - Recipe "Run sipnab as a HEP relay" in the cookbook is a relay that receives on `-L` and forwards on `-H`.
    - A bare flag would have no answer to "which half?".
    - That relay could not ask for TCP in and UDP out.
  - HEP v3 declares its own total length.
    - So a stream is packets laid end to end, with no framing of sipnab's invention.
    - That is what Homer's agents already send.
  - HEP v2 declares no total length.
    - So it cannot be delimited on a stream at all.
    - A `tcp` or `tls` listener reads v3 only, and says so rather than guessing.
  - A peer that sends anything else loses its connection.
    - sipnab does not try to resynchronize it.
    - A stream offers no point to resynchronize at.
    - One byte of slippage makes every later length garbage.
    - "Skip and continue" would silently discard everything that peer sent afterwards.
  - The listener serves several agents at once.
    - It uses one thread per connection inside a scope, so no reader outlives it.
  - It survives the two things a real estate does to a collector:
    - A peer whose packet arrives in two segments.
    - A peer that vanishes mid-packet.
  - The sender rebuilds its connection when the collector restarts.
    - It makes one attempt per packet, never a loop.
    - So a collector that is simply down does not turn forwarding into a spin.
  - The sender sets `TCP_NODELAY`.
    - These are small packets whose whole value is timeliness.
- **`--hep-tls-ca`, `--hep-tls-cert` and `--hep-tls-key`.**
  - The sender verifies the collector against `--hep-tls-ca`.
    - When none is named, it verifies against the host's CA bundle.
  - A named CA **replaces** the trust store rather than joining it.
    - A private collector's issuer is the whole of what that sender should accept.
  - A CA file that cannot be read or holds no certificate is an error.
    - It is not treated as an empty store.
    - An empty store would refuse everything and read as a broken far end.
  - The listener presents `--hep-tls-cert`/`--hep-tls-key`.
  - It refuses a private key any other user on the host can read.
  - The client handshake completes when the connection is dialed, not on the first packet.
    - rustls is lazy by default.
    - Without that, sipnab tells the operator forwarding is up.
    - Then the first SIP message an hour later discovers the certificate was never acceptable.

  - Some things are unchanged on every transport:
    - Authentication (`--hep-auth-file`, `--hep-auth-mode`).
    - The origin and security semantics (`input_origin: Hep`, `--hep-allow-kill`, `--hep-allow`).
    - They are one ingest path, not one per socket type.
  - Under TLS, `--hep-allow` still means the source address of the connection.
    - TLS does not make it redundant.
    - sipnab asks connecting agents for no certificate of their own.
    - So TLS says the path is private, and nothing about who is on it.
- **A transport or TLS flag whose side is not in the run is refused at
  startup.**
  - Of the three possible outcomes, `--hep-tls-ca` on a plaintext sender is the worst to accept silently:
    - The operator believes the feed is encrypted.
    - The exit status agrees with them.
    - The packets are in the clear.
  - Each refusal names the flag value that would make the flag live.

- **Twenty-one tests that drive the sockets rather than describe them.**
  - A test holds down each claim above.
    - It runs a real listener and a real sender over loopback.
  - The tests cover:
    - Whole packets end to end on TCP and on TLS.
    - A collector restart the sender rebuilds through.
    - Several agents at once.
    - A packet split across two writes.
    - A packet whose body has not all arrived yet.
    - A peer that vanishes mid-packet.
    - A stream that is not HEP v3.
    - The authentication and allowlist refusals on TCP.
  - Seventeen of those behaviors were then removed one at a time.

    - Each removal turned its test red.
  - In the listener and the sender:
    - The framer's short-buffer check.
    - The HEP3 magic check.
    - The private key's permission refusal.
    - The reconnect.
    - The CA replacement.
    - The accept-time allowlist.
    - The auth refusal.
    - Completing the handshake at dial.
  - On the command line:
    - The transport enum's default.
    - The sender's default.
    - The two refusals of a TLS flag on a plaintext side.
    - The refusal of a TLS listener with nothing to present.
    - The three `requires` clauses that stop a transport or TLS flag being accepted without the side it governs.
  - The tests did not catch two removals at first.
    - Both were the test's fault rather than the code's.
  - The split-packet test cut its buffer where a short read and a whole one look alike.

    - So a framer that ignored short buffers passed it.
    - The held-until-it-lands test cuts four bytes into the body, where they do not look alike.

  - The allowlist test asserted only that no packet reached the pipeline.
    - `admit`'s own per-packet allowlist guarantees that whether or not the connection was ever refused.
    - The test now reads the socket and requires the connection to have ended.
    - That is the part that keeps a rejected source from holding a reader thread open by saying nothing.
  - Its fixture hid the difference a second time.
    - `serve_hep_stream` counts every packet it reads toward `--count`, dropped ones included.
    - So a one-packet budget closed the connection for the wrong reason.

### Fixed

- **A HEP allowlist test failed on macOS for a reason that was not the
  behavior under test.**
  - It asked the peer socket for a read timeout after writing.
  - macOS returns `EINVAL` from `setsockopt(SO_RCVTIMEO)` once the peer has reset the connection.
    - That is exactly what the listener's refusal does.
    - It is exactly what the test arranges.
  - Linux tolerates the late call.
    - So it passed locally and on the Linux runners, and failed only on macOS.
  - The test now sets the timeout while the socket is plainly healthy, before the write.

    - The assertion no longer depends on which side wins the race.

- **The published binary-size ceiling moves 14 MB to 15 MB, because TLS costs
  space.**

  - The TLS transports added `rustls` to the `hep` feature.
  - That took the stripped x86_64 musl binary to 15,481,608 bytes -- 14.76 MiB.
    - That is over the 14 MB the homepage advertised.
  - The release gate compares the ceiling against the real artifact, not against another document.
    - So it failed the release rather than letting the claim drift.
    - That is the failure it was written for.
    - The homepage once said 5 MB against a 9.34 MB binary.
  - 15 rather than 16: it is the tightest bound that is still true.

    - The claim is worth more than the headroom.
  - That leaves about 247 KB.
    - So the next dependency of any size trips this again, deliberately.
    - The gate runs only at release time.
    - A loose ceiling would hide growth until it was large.

  - The number is single-sourced in `website/config.toml`.
  - The gate requires these to quote it:
    - The homepage tile.
    - The feature table.
    - Both build documents.

- **The TCP reconnect test encoded one platform's timing as if it were the
  behavior.**
  - The sender rebuilds its connection when a write fails.
  - A write fails only once the peer's RST is back.
  - How many writes that takes is the kernel's business.
    - On Linux the RST beats the second packet.
    - On macOS it does not.
  - The test sent a fixed three packets and then accepted.
    - That passed everywhere but the macOS runner.
    - There, no connection arrived inside ten seconds.
  - The test now offers packets until the sender reconnects.
    - The deadline is the failure.
    - The claim is that it rebuilds when the collector comes back.
    - The claim is not that it rebuilds on any particular packet.
  - A sender that never rebuilds still fails.

- **Two `rust/cleartext-logging` alerts, dismissed as false positives with the
  dataflow path recorded rather than by assertion.**
  - `hep_tls_sink` returns `(HepSink, SocketAddr)`.
  - The certificate material genuinely reaches the sink.
  - CodeQL then loses tuple-element precision.
    - It carries that taint onto the address element.
    - sipnab stores that element as `HepSender.local_addr` and formats it into an assert message.

  - The reported sink is a `SocketAddr`, which cannot hold PEM bytes.
  - Certificates are public material in any case.
  - The private-key path does not appear in the flow.
  - The alerts are new only because this release introduced `pem_certificates` as a taint source.


### Changed

- **Two claims about media-to-leg correlation now have tests that name them.**
  - Someone asked how sipnab ties an RTP quality problem back to the SIP leg causing it.
  - The answer given was that a later pass resolves streams whose packets arrived before their SDP.
  - On one worker that is not what happens.
    - Linking the SDP claims an already-seen stream itself.
    - The later pass exists for the merge case.
    - A separate test already covers that case.
  - A mutation caught the mistake.
    - Gutting that pass left the first draft of these tests green.
  - The tests now assert the real mechanism.
  - They also assert that a rival SDP for the same socket never steals a stream that already belongs to a call.

## [0.5.149] - 2026-09-03

### Fixed

- **The documentation instructed a peer command no released TFPS has.**
  - The TFPS surfaces shipped in 0.5.148 were built against a TFPS branch.
    - That branch adds JSON output and an `ingest` subcommand.
  - Nobody has merged that branch, and nobody has proposed it upstream.
  - So a reader following sipnab's own example piped findings into a `tfps_ctl` with no `ingest`.
  - They also read tool descriptions promising JSON a released `tfps_ctl` never emits.
  - Now:
    - The example no longer names an unreleased command.
    - Each surface says plainly which peer capability it waits for.
    - A gate fails any document that instructs a `tfps_ctl` subcommand or flag outside the released set.
  - A feature may ship ahead of its peer; instructions may not.

## [0.5.148] - 2026-09-03

### Added

- **`--evidence-out`: sipnab publishes findings, and something else decides.**
  - sipnab does not ban, and the reason stands.
    - A firewall entry is a state change on another system.
    - It has a lifetime sipnab neither sets nor knows.
  - That is an argument about who applies a ban.
    - It is not about who may say what they saw.
  - Every finding that names a source can now be written as JSON Lines.
    - A golden fixture fixes the shape.
    - The TFPS repository holds a byte-identical copy of that fixture.
    - It is for `| tfps_ctl ingest` or any other reader.
  - The sink opens when the run starts.
    - So an unwritable path is an error before the first packet.
  - A HEP-carried finding publishes nothing without `--hep-allow-kill`.
    - That is the same rule the jail log follows, for the same reason.
- **TFPS surfaces: six MCP tools, six REST routes, one locator.**
  - The toll-fraud prevention system (TFPS) may run beside sipnab.
    - It condemns sources and enforces the decision in the firewall.
  - sipnab never bans anything.
  - Until now, an agent reading `security_findings` could not see what TFPS did with the evidence without a shell on the box.
  - `tfps_status`, `tfps_banned`, `tfps_dropped` and `tfps_labels` read what TFPS knows.
  - `tfps_ban` and `tfps_unban` relay an OPERATOR's decision.
    - They report TFPS's answer as given.
    - A refusal (`self`, `ignoreip`, `not-blocked`, `invalid`) is an answer and not an error.
    - `tfps_ctl` signals a refusal with exit 1 beside the same structured line.

  - These routes answer the same shapes:
    - `GET /v1/tfps/status`, `/banned`, `/dropped`, `/labels`.
    - `POST /v1/tfps/ban`, `/unban`.
    - They are serialized from the same types, so the two doors cannot drift.
  - `--tfps-ctl PATH` and `[tfps] ctl` / `[tfps] db` say where `tfps_ctl` is.
    - When they are absent, sipnab looks on `PATH` only when a TFPS tool is called.
  - TFPS stays optional peer software. A machine without it:
    - Answers `installed: false` with a reason on every surface -- a result, not an error.
    - Runs unchanged.
    - Logs nothing about TFPS at startup.
  - The `no tfps in the manifest` gate still holds.
  - The TFPS emitter's own fixtures pin the contract.
    - They are copied byte for byte and held to their SHA-256.
    - The fixtures are `tfps-status-golden.json`, `tfps-banned-golden.jsonl`, `tfps-dropped-golden.jsonl`, `tfps-ban-golden.jsonl`, `tfps-unban-golden.jsonl`.
    - They also include the two evidence files the next entry emits and TFPS answers with.
    - Each is proved to parse: every field present, `null` where TFPS does not know.
  - Every argument sipnab sends follows `tfps_ctl`'s own grammar.
    - The arguments are separate `argv` elements, never a shell line.

  - The executable is an input to every test. It is a shell script that does one of these:
    - Echoes a fixture.
    - Exits 1 with a refusal.
    - Exits 3.
    - Is absent.

### Fixed

- **Nine CodeQL alerts, and the configuration that claimed to suppress them.**
  - `rust/hard-coded-cryptographic-value` flagged nine test fixtures in `digest_leak`.
    - They built a 401 challenge with a pasted nonce.

  - The CodeQL config excluded that rule "inside `#[cfg(test)]` modules" with `tags contain: test`.
    - That filters a query's metadata tags.
    - No security query carries one.
    - So the filter matched nothing.
    - The alerts rode through three tagged releases under a comment saying they were suppressed.
  - The fixtures now mint their nonces at runtime, memoized by label.
    - Equal labels compare equal, which is all the detector ever checks.
    - The first replacement was a hash seeded with a constant.
    - To the query, that was still a constant.
  - The config says plainly that inline test code cannot be excluded.

### Changed

- **Open code-scanning alerts block CI and block a tag, through one script.**
  - CodeQL ran as its own workflow, and its findings went to a tab.
  - The only required check was "CI success".
  - The tag hook checked CI but never alerts.
  - `scripts/code-scanning-clean.py` waits for CodeQL's analysis of the commit in question.
    - It fails on any open alert.
  - CI's aggregate requires it.
  - The pre-push tag check calls the same script.
  - A gate that cannot read the answer exits 2, never 0.
- **A local gate for pasted cryptographic material.**
  - It runs before the hook, in under a second.
  - No string literal may be handed to anything named nonce, secret, password, salt or a key assignment.
    - This applies in production code and in tests.
  - A fixture whose subject is the literal names itself with `// material: fixture -- <why>`.
  - Nothing else is exempt.
- **The homepage's standards band says what the code does, one card per
  standard.**
  - The "Quality Metrics" band carried six cards from the day it landed, laid out one per metric.
  - So G.107, RFC 3550 and RFC 3611 each headed two cards with different text.
    - Readers read that as a contradiction.
  - Nothing held any of them to `src/`:
    - The MOS card promised a 1-5 scale for an estimator that clamps to 4.5.
    - The "Burst / Gap Loss" card described `analyze_burst_gap`, which no surface calls.
    - Some outputs were emitted and never shown:
      - The round trip derived from RTCP.
      - The far end's own reception reports.
      - The G.113 impairment table.
      - The G.114 delay guidance.

  - The band is now five cards -- G.107, G.113, G.114, RFC 3550, RFC 3611.
    - Each is titled by the standard and linked to it.
    - Each lists the metrics it grounds.
  - A sibling "Standards Implemented" band does the same for SIP, SDP, RTP payload types, DTMF events, SRTP, TLS, STUN, HEP and vCon.
    - So a transport is not filed as a quality metric.
  - Ten gates in `tests/site_journey_test.rs` hold the cards to a canonical table. The table names:
    - The code symbol behind every item.
    - The field the program emits for every metric.
    - The exact string behind every specific claim.
    - A citation in both `docs/` and the built site mirror.
  - The gates enforce one card per standard.
  - A control page wrong in all nine ways must be reported for all nine.
- **`pplsip` is a known scanner signature.**
  - Measured on live traffic on 2026-09-03.
  - The TFPS peer banned a source for one INVITE to a toll-fraud number carrying `User-Agent: pplsip`.
  - sipnab's scanner detector let it through.
    - It knows `friendly-scanner` and `sipvicious`.
  - This adds one signature, because it was measured.
  - Nobody's list was imported wholesale.

- **The TFPS label harness names its sources.**
  - `tfps_label_corpus_test` reported "recalled 1 of 15" and nothing else.
  - Someone inferred the one recalled address by hand, backwards.
  - The score now carries the addresses under each outcome and prints them:
    - `recalled`
    - `missed`
    - `false_positives`
    - `flagged_unlabeled`
  - A miss is a hostile source that appears in the corpus and went unflagged.
  - A hostile source TFPS saw in a window the pcaps do not cover is not charged to the detector.

## [0.5.147] - 2026-09-03

### Added

- **`--fraud-destination <ISO,...>`: the fraud detector knows where a call is
  going.**
  - This is the one capability the cross-project review found missing.
    - Every heuristic reasoned about call shape.
    - None could say the destination.
  - A new `security::destination` module ports two things from the TFPS project:
    - Its dial-plan stripping.
    - Its longest-prefix country lookup.
  - The license is Apache-2.0.
  - It is ported rather than depended on.
    - So a machine without TFPS is unchanged.
    - The no-`tfps`-in-the-manifest gate still holds.
  - sipnab reports an INVITE to a watched country on sight.
  - Every fraud finding carries the resolved destination.
  - `+1 809` resolves to `DO`, not `US`.
  - A number with no international prefix is domestic and never matches.

### Fixed

- **`--hep-parse` no longer lets a forged inner source pass the origin gate.**
  - Unwrapping a HEP datagram read from a pcap or interface cloned the outer packet.
  - The remote HEP sender asserted the inner SIP's addressing.
  - So the inner SIP inherited `Wire`.
    - It was eligible for both a jail line and a kill response.

  - The origin gate closes that hole for `--hep-listen`.
  - It is now closed for `--hep-parse` too.
  - The unwrapped packet carries `InputOrigin::Hep`.
    - So a kill or jail line needs `--hep-allow-kill`, the same opt-in as the listener.

### Changed

- **Two gates for two ways a change slips its paperwork.**
  - Every `[security]` config key the program reads must have a row in `docs/config-reference.md`.
    - The docs-drift tests paired flags with their rows, never config keys.
    - A key was added, wired and tested without one.
  - `security::destination` must stay unconditional while `detectors` keeps its feature gate.
    - A scripted insert beneath the attribute line moved the gate onto the wrong module.

- **The manual pre-push path is pinned as stdin-safe.**

  - Run by hand, `.githooks/pre-push` blocks at its git-protocol refspec loop when stdin is left open.
    - That reads as a frozen gate.

  - Tests now hold `scripts/preflight.sh` free of any such loop.
    - That is the safe manual path.
  - Tests pin the hook's single stdin read to that one refspec loop.
    - So no future edit can add an earlier read that blocks a manual run before a gate prints.
  - The fix is to run `preflight.sh`, or push through git.
    - Do not invoke the hook directly.

## [0.5.146] - 2026-09-03

### Fixed

- **The abandoned-worktree gate could block every commit while a worktree was
  in use.**
  - Under `git commit`, the pre-commit hook inherits three variables for the repository being committed to:
    - `GIT_DIR`
    - `GIT_INDEX_FILE`
    - `GIT_WORK_TREE`
  - The gate's child `git status` started inside another worktree.
    - It inherited them too.
    - So it reported on the parent repository and called a live worktree empty.
  - It passed when run by hand, because by hand there was nothing to leak.
  - The probe now scrubs those variables.
  - A worktree whose work is committed but merged nowhere is no longer counted as abandoned.
- **`--fail2ban` no longer warns that the run will emit nothing when
  `--reg-flood` is armed.**
  - The startup warning about an empty jail log consulted the scanner detector alone.
  - So `sipnab -d eth0 --reg-flood --fail2ban -N` announced "this run will emit nothing".
    - Then it wrote `reg_flood src=` lines into the log it had just called empty.
  - The warning now consults every producer of a jail line:
    - A scanner detection.
    - A `-K`/`--kill-target` match.
    - A registration flood.
  - It prints only when all three are absent.
    - That is the rule the CLI reference already stated.
  - Its text names both detections and every flag that arms one.
- **`--hep-send` stamps each message with the transport it arrived on.**
  - The forwarding loop re-parsed every SIP message with a literal UDP transport before handing it to the sender.
  - So `-d eth0 --hep-send homer:9060` on a TCP or TLS trunk delivered every message with IP protocol 17.
    - The collector recorded the trunk as UDP.
  - The message now goes as the pipeline delivered it: addresses, ports, transport and timestamp.
    - 6 for TCP, TLS and WebSocket.
    - 17 for UDP.
    - 132 for SCTP.
    - This is exactly as RTCP already did.
  - The second parse of every message on the hot path is gone with it.
  - The forwarding decision lives in one function a test can reach.
  - A message the first-line check recognizes as SIP now reaches the collector even when the full parser rejects it.
    - A malformed message is something the collector should see, not something to hide.

- **A spoofed-source flood no longer makes every later packet pay for a scan
  of the detector maps.**
  - Each security detector caps its per-source map at ten thousand entries.
  - Each one chose the entry to evict with `min_by_key` over the whole map.
    - That is ten thousand comparisons per packet once the map was full.
    - It ran on the capture thread.
    - It ran inside the per-packet critical section that holds both store write locks.
    - Meanwhile every MCP and API reader waited, and the kernel's drop counter climbed.
  - These now evict their least recently used entry in constant time:
    - The registration flood, scanner and fraud detectors' source maps.
    - The alert engine's cooldown, event and per-source exec-budget maps.
    - The flood detector's per-source open transactions.
  - Measured on the flood detector:
    - Admitting a source to a full map cost 371 times what admitting one to an empty map cost.
    - It now costs 1.3 times.
  - The alert engine's event map was also only trimmed after a key reached its rule's threshold.
    - Under a rule like `scanner:5/1m`, a flood of sources that each fired once grew it without bound.
    - It is now bounded by construction.

- **`--digest-leak` no longer reports a retransmitted 401 as nonce reuse.**

  - The detector kept one set of nonces with no notion of a transaction.
  - Consider a REGISTER over lossy UDP whose 401 was lost.
    - The client retransmits.
    - Section 17.2.2 of RFC 3261 requires the registrar to answer with the same final response.

  - That produced `nonce reused across challenges (replay risk)` against a healthy registrar.
    - `--alert-exec` spawned a command for it.
  - sipnab now remembers a nonce with the transaction it was issued on.
    - The transaction is the Call-ID, CSeq and top Via branch.
  - The same nonce on that transaction again is the retransmission and counts for nothing.
  - The same nonce on any other transaction is still reported, once.

- **`--reg-flood` no longer reports a registrar's own customers.**
  - The detector counted REGISTERs.
  - It fired when the count from one source crossed the threshold.
  - Consider a customer SBC re-registering two hundred phones after a registrar restart.
    - The registrar answered every one `200 OK`.
    - That produced a `reg_flood` line.
    - `--fail2ban` handed the trunk to the firewall.
  - It now counts challenged failures.
    - A challenged failure is a REGISTER that carried `Authorization` or `Proxy-Authorization` and drew a `401` or `407` on the same transaction.
  - A REGISTER on its own is never evidence.
  - A challenge to a REGISTER without credentials is the first half of every registration.
    - It counts for nothing.
  - Any `2xx` to a REGISTER clears the source's count.
  - The alert and the fail2ban line carry the failure count that crossed the threshold.
  - The alert detail reads `auth_failures=N registers=M threshold=T`.

- **`--reg-flood` measures its window in capture time.**
  - It used the wall clock.
  - `sipnab -I yesterday.pcap --reg-flood --fail2ban -N` reads a file as fast as the disk delivers it.
  - So it saw a phone that re-registered once a minute for an hour as sixty REGISTERs in one second.
    - It wrote a ban line for it.
  - The window and the sweep now follow the packets' own timestamps.
    - The scanner detector already did this.
  - So a file replays as the traffic it recorded.

- **A 401 flood cannot exhaust the registration flood detector's memory.**
  - The cap on tracked sources applied only where a REGISTER created an entry.
  - A `401` or `407` toward any destination created one too, uncapped.
    - So a flood of challenges aimed at a /16 of addresses grew the map without bound before the first sweep.
  - A response now updates an existing source's state and never creates one.
  - A flood of responses can no longer evict a source in the middle of the brute force it is counting.

- **`--fail2ban` no longer writes jail lines for detections carried by HEP
  unless `--hep-allow-kill` is set.**
  - A HEP sender asserts the inner source and destination addresses.
  - The kill path has refused to act on that claim without the opt-in since SN-01.
  - The ban path wrote the line regardless.
  - Consider `--hep-listen 0.0.0.0:9060 --hep-allow 198.51.100.0/24 --reg-flood --fail2ban`.
    - Any host in that range could send HEP-wrapped REGISTERs naming the customer's SBC as their source.
    - So could a UDP source spoofed into that range.
    - The jail would then ban the SBC.
  - All three jail-line sites now pass the same origin predicate as the kill path.
    - The sites are scanner detection, `-K` match and registration flood.
  - The predicate:
    - Wire-origin traffic is always written.
    - HEP-origin traffic is written only under `--hep-allow-kill`.
    - Uprobe-origin traffic is never written.
  - The finding itself still reaches the alert path.
  - A run that pairs `--fail2ban` with HEP input and no opt-in says at startup that its jail log stays empty by design.
- **Two gates read the wrong repository from inside a hook.**
  - Under `git commit`, the pre-commit hook inherits `GIT_DIR`, `GIT_INDEX_FILE` and `GIT_WORK_TREE` for the repository being committed to.
  - A child `git` started in another directory inherits them too.
  - The abandoned-worktree gate reported on the parent.
    - It blocked every commit while a worktree was in use.

  - The staged-inputs gate's fixtures staged into the parent's temporary index during a partial commit.
  - Both now scrub those variables before they spawn git.

### Changed

- **The production-panic gate now covers the macro spellings of "abort here".**
  - `scripts/check-unwrap.py` banned `.unwrap()` and `.expect()` on production paths and nothing else.
  - `panic!`, `unreachable!`, `todo!` and `unimplemented!` end the process exactly as an unwrap does.
  - A clippy restriction-lint measurement found:
    - Zero of the former under `src/`.
    - Nine sites of the latter that no gate had ever looked at.
  - The gate now reports all four macros.
  - A site that genuinely cannot be reached keeps the macro only with a comment on the line above it.
    - The comment is `// gate: <macro> because <reason>`.
    - The marker must name the macro it covers and give a reason.
    - The gate reports a marker that gives no reason rather than honoring it.
  - Of the nine sites, two are rewritten so the macro is gone:
    - `rtpengine::ng::parse` decides the body's kind in one match.
    - `header_form::reformat_headers` treats the as-captured mode as "leave the name alone", which is what it already did.
  - Seven carry a reason.
    - Each was re-read to confirm no wire or user input reaches it.

- **Fuzz targets for the STUN and LLMNR decoders.**
  - `stun::parse` and the ChannelData framing checks run on every UDP datagram that is not SIP.
  - `llmnr::parser::parse_llmnr` runs on every datagram touching port 5355.
  - Neither had a coverage-guided target.
  - `fuzz_stun` and `fuzz_llmnr` join the weekly run.
  - The always-on smoke fuzz in `cargo test` drives the same entry points.
  - Sixty seconds of each locally produced no crash.
  - The weekly workflow's matrix now lists every target.
    - It had never listed `fuzz_rtpengine_ng`, which landed after the matrix was last edited.
- **A tracked file may not carry a merge-conflict marker.**
  - A squash left `<<<<<<<`/`>>>>>>>` in two files, and they were staged.
  - fmt, Vale, codespell, clippy and the whole suite ran over them without noticing.
  - A gate now scans every tracked text file for the two markers that never occur legitimately.

### Changed

- **The security detectors run as one function that returns what should
  happen.**
  - `process_parsed_packet` in the batch loop ran these checks inline:
    - The scanner.
    - `--kill-target`.
    - Fraud.
    - Digest-leak.
    - Registration-flood.
  - It filed findings, wrote jail lines and handed responses to the kill worker.
    - That took a hundred and thirty lines of a function over five hundred lines long.
  - So only a test that drove the whole loop could see the wiring of each detector.
  - `security::detectors::run_detectors` now takes these inputs:
    - The armed detectors.
    - The message.
    - Its dialog.
    - The run's policy.
  - It returns a list of effects that the loop applies:
    - A finding to file.
    - A jail line to write.
    - A kill to send.
  - Behavior is unchanged:
    - The same checks run in the same order.
    - The origin gate sits at the same five points.
    - Every rule name is still assigned where the finding is filed.
  - Each wire has a unit test of its own.

## [0.5.145] - 2026-09-03

### Added

- **`scanner_detect` can be scored against an external oracle.**

  - [Section 7, "Recommendation", of `docs/design/threat-mitigation-hooks.md`](docs/design/threat-mitigation-hooks.md#7-recommendation) names a prerequisite.

    - The prerequisite is a labeled corpus: real traffic with known scanners marked.
    - It is measured for both false-positive and false-negative rate.
    - It is the prerequisite for every automated-response decision this project has deferred.
  - That section says sipnab cannot build one alone.
    - Nothing in a capture says which source was hostile.
  - A new corpus test reads labels exported by an external enforcement tool.
    - It scores the detector against them.
  - It sits alongside the existing suite.

    - That suite scores alerts against an oracle derived from the packets themselves.
  - The tool supplying those labels is optional software.
    - It is in the same category as rtpengine, OpenSIPS or Kamailio.
    - A machine might run several, or none.

  - There is no new dependency in the manifest.
  - The labels are read as plain JSON, and a test asserts it stays that way.
  - With nothing configured the suite skips.
    - Its sibling does the same without `SIPNAB_CORPUS`.

### Changed

- **The comparison framing no longer names two specific tools.**
  - These described flags, TUI conventions and positioning by reference to two other projects by name:
    - Documentation.
    - Help text.
    - Code comments.
    - The site.

  - The behavior they described is unchanged.
    - It is now described on its own terms.
  - One internal CLI field was renamed with them.
  - No user-facing flag changed.
  - The hidden `-r` compatibility no-op still works exactly as before.

- The corpus capture reader moved to `tests/support/corpus.rs`.
  - A second suite needed it.
  - A corpus walker copied into two files agrees until one of them learns about a new capture format.

### Fixed

- **`--export-vcon-when` accepts the aliases `--filter` accepts.**
  - `cli-reference.md` says the flag takes "the language `--filter` already speaks".
  - But `--filter problems` exited 0 and `--export-vcon-when problems` exited 1.

    config)`.

  - `RunPlan` now carries the resolved predicate.

  - A gate walks every flag whose help claims the filter language.
    - It requires the plan to resolve it.

### Changed

- **Backlog bookkeeping only; nothing here reaches a binary.**
  - RDX1 and RDX2 shipped in 0.5.143.
  - Their entries were never checked off.
  - So the status table said 28 open while two of them were released.

  - Two looked closeable and were not:
